title: ‘Bush v. Gore’ in Missouri? Congressional map showdown pits state law against federal law - kctv5.com
content: KANSAS CITY, Mo. (KCTV) - A “battle of the maps” is ensuing in the Show Me State as the nation’s eyes turn to a highly anticipated Missouri Supreme Court hearing Thursday morning. Missouri’s state courts and federal courts are locked in a historic jurisdictional standoff over which congressional map will govern the upcoming midterm election. The tension has escalated so far that the state’s highest court has ordered Secretary of State Denny Hoskins to return to Jefferson City immediately to explain in person why he should not be held in contempt of court. Political analysts liken the showdown to the 2000 election and Bush vs. Gore. This November’s midterm election will be closely watched as the balance of power in Congress could shift. Missouri’s congressional map could make the difference of one seat for either the Republican or Democratic party in the U.S. House of Representatives. The map in question decides who represents Missourians in the U.S. House of Representatives. Missouri lawmakers drew a new congressional map during a special session last year. The 2025 map carves up the Kansas City area into three districts, creating a map that favors sending a Republican to Washington D.C. over current Democratic Congressman Emanuel Cleaver. This was part of a national redistricting back-and-forth between Republicans and Democrats as the 2026 midterm election could change the balance of power in the U.S. House. A veto petition challenging the map gathered more than 300,000 signatures. If approved, the petition would put the 2025 map on pause, revert voters to the map drawn in 2022, and put a question on the November ballot for voters to decide which map to use going forward. Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected that petition on the same day as the August primary election, leading to the state lawsuit. The primary election was conducted under the new 2025 map, although a previous ruling from the Missouri Supreme Court said that map would have never gone into effect if the petition was found to have enough valid signatures. The conflict centers on two competing maps. The Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the state must use the 2022 congressional map for the upcoming election, tossing out a new map drawn last year to favor Republicans (HB 1). However, a federal district judge subsequently issued a Temporary Restraining Order (TRO) enjoining Hoskins from using any map other than the Republican-drawn HB 1 map, citing federal constitutional and equal protection grounds for voters who already voted in the primaries under those boundaries. Following the federal order, Hoskins immediately instructed local election clerks to proceed with the HB 1 map. Hoskins was at the airport Wednesday, cutting his trip to the Republican National Convention in Dallas short to be back in Missouri for the state court hearing Thursday morning. Speaking at the airport, Hoskins defended his decision by invoking federal supremacy. “The Supremacy Clause, where if you read Article 6 Clause 2 of the US Constitution, it basically says where federal law and state law conflict, the federal wins,” Hoskins said. When asked about the ongoing legal drama, Hoskins insisted he did his job properly. “I would say I met every state law deadline, I met every constitutional deadline,” Hoskins said. “There’s a reason we have deadlines and I met the deadline.” Meanwhile, the federal court case continues through court filings. People Not Politicians elevated their appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, asking Judge Brett Kavanaugh to respond by 9 a.m. Missouri-time Thursday. Hoskins is facing off against People Not Politicians, the citizen activist group that successfully fought to strike down the Republican-favored map in state court. Their attorney, Chuck Hatfield, strongly rejects the argument that federal law overrides the state supreme court’s authority in this instance. “This issue is a matter of state law, there are what we call in the business, independent state grounds for this decision, it is not a matter of federal law,” Hatfield said. In a newly submitted suggestions filing, Hatfield urged the state supreme court to hold Hoskins in civil contempt. Hatfield argued that Hoskins’ team actively ginned up the “friendly” federal lawsuit to manufacture a conflict and bypass the state’s highest authority. In filings, Hatfield suggested the court bypass Hoskins entirely by directly ordering local election authorities not to use the HB 1 map. Legal experts and political analysts agree that the clash between state and federal jurisdictions is an extraordinary and rare scenario. Former Missouri Supreme Court Justice Mike Wolff likened the situation to one of the most famous election disputes in U.S. history. “It really feels like Bush versus Gore,” Wolff said. “’Cause in that case, Florida courts were adjudicating the count of votes in Florida, and the U.S. Supreme Court stepped in and said, ‘Oh wait a minute, there’s gonna be an equal protection problem here.’” However, Wolff emphasized that because state laws generally govern elections, Hoskins remains legally answerable to the state court system. “I think the question for Hoskins is, do you have an obligation to obey the orders of the Supreme Court of Missouri? And the answer to that is a resounding yes,” Wolff said. As for what happens next at tomorrow’s hearing, Wolff admitted, “Especially in this situation, who knows?” Nathan Carrington, PhD, a political scientist at Saint Louis University, agrees that the issue will likely land on the steps of the nation’s highest court. “Who knows where this is going to end up. I do think this is going to go back to the Supreme Court in some way, I don’t think they’re gonna be able to dodge it the way they did before,” Carrington said. With the high-stakes hearing scheduled for Thursday, time is rapidly running out for local election officials. Local clerks are hoping for immediate clarity. They are currently working against a tight deadline to prepare and mail out November absentee ballots starting next week. “Time is of the essence and the courts are aware of that, so whatever is going to happen is probably going to happen pretty quick in the next few days,” Carrington noted.

title: Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V - The Guardian
content: Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close Norway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of ​national mourning that followed the popular monarch’s death last month at the age of 89. Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades. With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress. King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked in the cortege, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car. The procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; ‌Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”. The prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.” After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony. Norwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss ⁠classes for the occasion. The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Harald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particular coming under heavy criticism – including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pallbearer during the transfer to the royal chapel. Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK.

title: The World’s Royal Families Converged in Norway for the Funeral of King Harald V - Vanity Fair
content: Currently, only residents from GDPR countries and certain US states can opt out of Tracking Technologies through our Consent Management Platform. The eyes of the world were on Norway Wednesday, as the country bid farewell to King Harald V with a grand state funeral at Oslo Cathedral. The day marked the culmination of the period of national mourning that followed the death of the monarch, who passed away on August 28 at the age of 89. Like the 2022 funeral for Queen Elizabeth II in the United Kingdom, Harald V’s funeral attracted supporters from royal families from all over the world, including the UK, Sweden, Denmark, Greece, Belgium, Spain, and Japan. Prince William and Princess Anne traveled from the UK for the occasion—the Windsors and the Norwegian royal family are related through shared ancestry traced to Queen Victoria. Harald’s death has occurred during a complicated time for the Norwegian royal family, and the events surrounding the funeral have attracted national and global media interest. See pictures from the funeral below, along with a list of the foreign emissaries who attended. King Harald’s coffin, with the royal family behind it in the procession In recent days, thousands of people across the country have paid tribute to the popular king by bringing flowers, lighting candles, and leaving messages of condolence. The Royal Palace in Oslo has become the center of national mourning, and a massive memorial made of mementos has spontaneously formed in the square in front of it. The entrance to Oslo Cathedral was prepared for the occasion. A large canopy was erected in front of the church doors to welcome those attending the ceremony. The structure was decorated with fir branches and purple fabric—two elements chosen for their strong symbolic meaning. Dean Pål Kristian Balstad explained that the fir tree evokes the idea of evergreen life and eternity, but also has a special connection to the late monarch. “King Harald loved nature and was a man who adored being outdoors,” he recalled. Purple, too, has a specific symbolic function. It is the color traditionally associated with mourning and sadness. King Haakon of Norway with Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, Prince Sverre Magnus, and Princess Martha Louise. King Harald’s final journey began at the Royal Palace at noon. From there, the casket set out, accompanied by King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, Prince Sverre Magnus, and Princess Märtha Louise, who followed on foot. Queen Mette-Marit and Queen Sonja, meanwhile, rode in the A-2, a custom limousine used by the royal family. Other family members were also present, from shaman Durek Verrett to Princess Märtha Louise’s daughters, to Marius Borg Høiby, Queen Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship. Høiby’s presence at the event was noteworthy—in June, he was convicted of two counts of rape and is currently awaiting a four-year sentence. Police allowed him to attend funeral events as he awaits an appeal. The procession moved slowly, about 60 steps per minute. The king’s aides stood beside the casket. Foreign royals also took part in the procession, arranged in order of length of reign, with the reigning monarchs at the front, followed by the heirs to the throne, heads of state, ministers, and Norwegian officials. The Norwegians witnessed a similar scene 35 years ago, when the entire country bid farewell to King Olav in 1991. On that occasion, the funeral procession moved slowly through Oslo, followed by a large crowd, and the ceremony was attended by representatives from over 100 countries, including heads of state, members of royal families, and diplomats. Among them was the then Vice President of the United States, Dan Quayle. Prince William and Princess Anne of the United Kingdom. On Wednesday, too, the route brought thousands of citizens to bid their final goodbye to King Harald. A massive security operation was organized, involving police forces from other parts of Norway, as well as personnel from the Armed Forces. Norway also requested security assistance from neighboring Sweden: K-9 units specializing in explosive detection were made available to the Norwegian police. The Nordic countries often share security resources during major events. Dowager Queen Sonja married King Harald as a commoner in 1968. Her daughter-in-law, Queen Mette-Marit, joined her in the A-2 limo for the funeral procession. The coffin was draped in the red royal standard and carried on a gun carriage, pulled by a military Mercedes-Benz G-Class. Along the entire route, from the Royal Palace to the cathedral and then on to Akershus Fortress, approximately 1,900 soldiers were lined up on both sides of the street. At 12:00 p.m., 21 salutes were fired from military posts across the country, with a 30-second pause between each shot. The Norwegian royal family—King Haakon VIII, Queen Mette-Marit, Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Prince Sverre Magnus—took their seats in the cathedral to the right of the casket. In the second row, Princess Märtha Louise, her husband Durek Verrett, and her three daughters—Maud Angelica, Leah Isadora, and Emma Tallulah—took their seats. In the front row, on the opposite side from the Norwegian royal family, sat the monarchs of Sweden and Denmark, along with the Jordanian royals. When the casket was carried into the cathedral, all the guests stood. The choir sang a hymn to mark the start of the ceremony, which continued with a minute of silence observed throughout the country. It was a deeply moving moment. Queen Sonja, Queen Mette-Marit, Märtha Louise, and Ingrid Alexandra each cried during Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre’s commemorative speech. Queen Sonja eventually placed a red rose on the casket to bid farewell to her beloved husband. Outside the cathedral, a large crowd followed the ceremony via loudspeakers. The atmosphere remained solemn and emotional, with many people huddled together in silence. Soldiers were also lined up in mourning formation. The guest list made the funeral one of the largest recent gatherings of the world’s royalty. Representatives of European royal houses and heads of state arrived in Oslo, along with family members and close friends of the Norwegian royal family. The presence of foreign monarchs and dignitaries underscores the role King Harald played on the international stage during his 35-year reign. Most of the royals are staying at the Grand Hotel in downtown Oslo and traveled to the Royal Palace by bus. Meanwhile, as a gesture of the utmost respect for the late monarch, the royal palaces in Madrid, Monaco, and elsewhere flew their flags at half-mast. Invitations to attend the funeral were extended to all countries with diplomatic representation in Oslo, as well as to member states of NATO, the EU, and the European Economic Area that do not have diplomatic representation in Norway. There is a specific international diplomatic protocol that establishes the order and precedence of the guests. Their position depends on several factors, including rank, closeness to the monarch, length of reign, and institutional role. King Frederik X and Queen Mary of Denmark were among the first royals to confirm their attendance at the funeral. The decision led to the postponement of their state visit to Belgium, originally scheduled for September 8–10. The official trip will take place at a later date, which has not yet been announced. The couple is staying on the royal yacht moored at the port of Oslo. Queen Margrethe, a third cousin of the late King Harald, was also supposed to be there but was unable to attend due to recent health challenges. King Frederik X of Denmark was among the first royals to remember his uncle with particular affection. “He was a wonderful uncle to me,” the Danish monarch said, describing him as someone who was “always in a good mood and affable, ” capable of “always making the right comment.” Frederik then addressed a message to the new King Haakon: “He will be a good king, and I look forward to helping him in any way I can.” Also present were Crown Prince Christian, Princess Benedikte, and Anna Maria of Greece, accompanied by their children Pavlos, Nikolaos, and Alexia. The Swedish royal family was present in full: King Carl Gustav, Queen Silvia, Princess Victoria, Prince Daniel, Prince Carl Philip, Princess Sofia, Princess Madeleine, and her husband Christopher O’Neill. The King of Sweden, who is King Haakon’s godfather, sent a telegram to the new monarch, describing Harald’s death as “a heavy blow” for Norway and assuring Haakon of the support of the royal family and the entire Swedish people. Relations between the Swedish and Norwegian royal families are particularly close. King Harald’s mother, Princess Märtha, was in fact Swedish. Furthermore, King Harald and King Carl Gustaf served as godparents to each other’s heirs to the throne. During the funeral service, Princess Victoria read a prayer in memory of King Harald V. Representing the Dutch royal family were King Willem-Alexander, Queen Máxima, the Crown Princess of the Netherlands, and Princess Beatrice, who was a dear friend of King Harald. Also present for the final farewell to King Harald were Grand Duke Guillaume and Grand Duchess Stèphanie of Luxembourg, as well as Grand Duke Henri. Representing the Spanish royal family were King Felipe VI, Queen Letizia, and Queen Sofia, the king’s mother. The presence of Queen Emerita added special significance to the delegation: Sofia, like other European queens of her generation, shares personal and family ties that have bound the continent’s royal houses for decades. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium also attend the funeral. Their presence holds special significance: Last March, the couple made a state visit to Norway and were received by King Harald himself. King Willem-Alexander of the Netherlands with Queen Máxima and Crown Princess Catharina Amalia. Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko of Japan were sent as representatives of Emperor Naruhito. Emperor Naruhito had attended the funeral of King Olav V—Harald’s father—in 1991, and last June, he met with Crown Prince Haakon during the latter’s visit to Tokyo. Crown Prince Alois and Crown Princess Sophie represented the small country of Liechtenstein. From the principality of Monaco came Prince Albert with Princess Charlene, and from Jordan, King Abdullah arrived with Queen Rania. Prince Kyril of Bulgaria, a close friend of King Haakon of Norway with whom he shares a passion for surfing, also made sure not to miss the event, accompanied by Princess Rosario. Also in attendance were Prince Alexander of Serbia and Princess Katherine. Turki Bin Mohammed Bin Fahd Bin Abdulaziz Al Saud arrived from Saudi Arabia. From the United Kingdom came Prince William, representing his father King Charles III, and Princess Anne. The latter, who is King Haakon VIII’s godmother, attended in a private capacity. King Harald and King Charles III were cousins, and the British monarch referred to Harald as his “dear cousin” when, following his death, he sent his condolences to the Norwegian royal family. The Vatican was represented by Cardinal Christophe Pierre, the Pope’s envoy, and Archbishop Julio Murat, the apostolic nuncio to Norway. Representatives of various religious denominations and faith communities in the country also attended the ceremony. Among the heads of state, the presence of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and first lady Olena Zelens’ka stood out. Among the members of the Norwegian royal family present Wednesday at the king’s funeral was Marius Borg Høiby, the son from Queen Mette-Marit of Norway’s first marriage, who was granted special permission. Marius’s house arrest has, in fact, been extended beyond the date of his step-grandfather’s funeral, King Harald V. The order, which was set to end on September 7, will remain in effect until the conclusion of the funeral ceremonies. Marius Borg Høiby has been under house arrest since last July, after being sentenced to four years in prison for two counts of rape and other crimes. The defense has filed an appeal against the most serious parts of the verdict, which are therefore not final. After spending some time in prison, Høiby was transferred to the royal residence at Skaugum, where he lives with an electronic ankle monitor. Prosecutors have repeatedly argued that there is a risk of reoffending, a claim firmly rejected by the defense. Marius also attended other memorial services for King Harald that took place in recent days, sparking some controversy. In particular, he was present at the procession alongside King Haakon and other members of the royal family, who carried the monarch’s casket from the Red Hall to the Palace Chapel, where it lay in state until the day of the funeral. King Haakon VIII and Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra led the procession. It passed through the Yellow Hall, the Hall of Mirrors, the Dining Room, the Small Banquet Hall, and finally the Grand Banquet Hall. Queen Mette-Marit and Queen Sonja, who were holding hands, also took part. Subsequently, the chapel was opened to the public for the “defilering,” the traditional procession past the casket, which allowed citizens to stop and pay their last respects to the king. After the religious service at Oslo Cathedral, the casket was escorted in a second, smaller procession to Akershus Fortress, where a private ceremony took place. This second part of the funeral is reserved primarily for the royal family, members of other European royal families, and a few representatives of the Norwegian authorities. This marked the conclusion of the funeral rites. King Harald was then laid to rest in the Royal Mausoleum at Akershus, the official burial chapel of the Norwegian royal family. Here, a final moment of reflection took place before the interment. The coffin was lowered into the crypt of the Royal Mausoleum, where it was placed alongside the sarcophagi of Harald’s parents and grandparents: King Olav V and Princess Märtha, and King Haakon VII and Queen Maud. At the end of the ceremony, when King Haakon VIII exited the church at Akershus Castle, the flags were once again raised to full height, bringing the period of national mourning for the monarch’s death to a close. A total of 42 gun salutes were then fired, divided into two salutes of 21 shots each, with a one-minute pause between them. Shaman Durek Verrett with one of Princess Martha Louise’s daughters, Maud Angelica Behn Immediately afterward, church bells across the country rang continuously for one hour to celebrate the beginning of the new reign. At the conclusion of the ceremonies, the royal family returned to the Royal Palace, following the same route taken by the funeral procession. Once back at the palace, King Haakon, Queen Mette-Marit, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, Queen Sonja, and Prince Sverre Magnus appeared on the balcony of the Royal Palace, symbolically marking the end of the day of mourning and the beginning of a new chapter for the Norwegian monarchy. King Frederik of Denmark with Queen Mary and Crown Prince Christian While the private ceremony took place at Akershus, another official celebration was scheduled at Oslo City Hall, organized by the Norwegian government and presided over by Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide. About 450 guests attended, including several foreign heads of state, government officials, representatives of institutions, and prominent Norwegian and international figures. City Hall, one of the Norwegian capital’s most iconic buildings, was chosen in part for its security features and its strong institutional significance. It’s actually the same building where the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded each year. Finally, following the public and private ceremonies, a reception was held at the Royal Palace. Harald V’s funeral marked the end of an era in Norway. Now, the reign of King Haakon VIII officially begins, as he is now called upon to carry on his father’s precious legacy. title: Here’s How Much Fuel I Saved Swapping My Subaru Forester For A Honda CR-V Hybrid - The Autopian
content:
It’s been a little more than two years since I chucked my 2016 Subaru Forester, which I didn’t love, for a 2024 Honda CR-V Hybrid AWD my family has nicknamed ‘Big Red.’ I’ve driven it almost 18,000 miles in that time, and have used a little under 500 gallons of fuel. While my decision wasn’t primarily motivated by saving fuel, I am curious how I’ve done so far. If you missed the whole saga of my Forester, most of my issues revolved around small maintenance issues and overall disappointing quality. The CVT was underwhelming in the way most CVTs from that era are, and the fuel economy was an abysmal 24 MPG lifetime by the time I decided to sell it. Now that I’ve had the CR-V for a while, I can do the math to determine whether or not this makes any economic sense purely on the basis of sipping gas. Above is what my Forester looked brand new and, as I remember it, what it looked like when I got rid of it. Just a totally decent crossover. What’s curious about Subaru is that it sort of gives off this vibe of being efficient, but many of its vehicles end up being a little below average. With the introduction of hybrids, Subaru has fixed a lot of its own issues in this regard (and the hybrid is definitely the one to get). The goal, though, is to compare it to my older vehicle. With the CR-V Hybrid, I’ve tracked the fuel economy very closely since first getting the vehicle. The total number of vehicle miles driven since acquiring the car in the summer of 2024 has been 17,874, but the first 52 miles were before I started tracking, so my fuel economy estimate is based on 17,822.9 miles. In that time, I’ve used one gallon of gas for every 37.5 miles driven, for an MPG of 37.5 and a total fuel usage of 475.3 gallons. This is almost dead-on where the EPA estimate is. Assuming an average cost of $3.55, my total money spent on fuel was about $1,687.23. I didn’t track fuel economy for the full life of the Subaru, but once I decided to start tracking it, I ended up with an average of 24 MPG. If I’d kept the Subaru and driven the same amount, that would have required 742.6 gallons of fuel, or $2,636.30, which means in a little more than two years I’ve saved about $949.07, or roughly a car payment each year. That’s not nothing, but it’s not really a big enough savings in just gasoline to justfy getting rid of the Subaru. I did sell the car at a good time and got a high value for my resale (another nice thing I can say about my Forester), so there was a secondary benefit there. If fuel prices get closer to averaging $4.00, then that’s about $500 a year in savings. Gas prices would have to get to $6.00 a gallon before I’m saving enough money each year to feel like it made sense on fuel savings alone, and even then it’s a stretch. Ok, what if I’d have gotten a CR-V non-hybrid instead of a CR-V Hybrid? At the time, a CR-V non-hybrid got 29 MPG combined and cost about $3,000 less. At an average of $3.55 a gallon, that’s $494.53 saved. At an average fuel cost of $4.00 a gallon, it’s $557.22. Not great, not terrible. Because I don’t drive the exact same amount each year, it’s maybe easier to figure this out by looking at a per-mile cost. At $4.00 a gallon, I spend about $0.107 per mile driven in my CR-V Hybrid. The non-hybrid CR-V is $0.138, and the Forester is $0.148. I’ve already made up $557.22 of my delta in this scenario, so I just need to make up $2,443. That comes to a break-even around 80,000 miles, which isn’t bad. If gas prices go down, then it’ll be a little longer, but I plan to own this vehicle until at least 100,000 miles. At that distance, I’ll eventually be quite happy with my decision. So far, I’ve put 4,422.7 miles on Big Red since it turned warm in roughly April of this year, and I’ve done an incredible 39.8 MPG over that period. At the end of a very cold winter, I saw the car’s MPG drop closer to 34 MPG. Hybrids, like electric cars, tend to perform worse in the winter, and Big Red has not been an exception. If it’s a mild winter, I may luck out and improve, or at least maintain, my current high fuel economy. I think I’m also driving more efficiently. As I wrote shortly after getting the CR-V, the game I play with myself is trying to see how long I can go just on battery power. That’s still something I do because of the car, so I think it gets credit. I’m happier overall with the CR-V than the Forester, have spent less at my local Honda dealer than I did at the Subaru dealership, and don’t have to deal with CVT woes on account of the CR-V not really having a transmission. The Forester handled a little better, but the slightly softer ride in the Honda more than makes up for it in city driving. With gas prices being where they are, getting more than 500 miles out of a tank of gas also just feels better, even if the economics of it don’t necessarily justify making the switch purely for fuel economy reasons. That’s all well and good, but my numbers guys say otherwise. According to those fine lads and lasses, they claim a fuel shark will outperform that by eleventeen frillion percent. I swapped a Forester for a CR-V for exactly the same reasons; even my 2016 CR-V gets a consistent 28mpg with mostly city driving while the 2005 Forester manual was like 23 on the highway. Subaru Forester might be vehicle that most fits  the old boat idom. The happiest day with them is buying and getting rid of them. Subaru dealers still calling me trying to sell me new Forester they sitting on tons of them. Still, it’s nice knowing you’ve put less CO2 into the atmosphere, which has a value. What you’ve perfectly illustrated is that there is zero financial sense to trade-in a functional car, on the premise of fuel savings alone. But when you do look to buy a new (to you) car, you should definitely consider fuel consumption. Depends… Going from an 8mpg truck to a 20mpg truck saves you 750 gallons of fuel over 10k miles (1250 vs 500), but switching from a 30mpg car to a 40mpg car saves you 83 gallons (333 vs 250). 750 gallons per year is painful, 83 is a rounding error. In this situation there is more then just fuel savings. Forester would bite you in the ass before long. It’s best to get rid of the pos while it still has some value. Functional enough to pawn off on some poor sob. That’s a Forester whole life. I know car prices and loans are out of control, but equating almost $950 to a single car payment feels insane. Given about 1 in 5 new loans has $1,000 (or more) per month payments, it is (sadly) not as insane as you’d think. We have a ’26 CRV Sport Hybrid 2WD bought nearly a year ago.  We have gotten 41 mpg since new, 75% highway driving in AZ.  Just around town it’s over 44mpg.  The torque is excellent in stop and go traffic. Why is the Autopian, the world’s best automotive site, always comparing EVs and Hybrids, and ICE cars solely thru mpg, and not adding the cost of the electricity? Then not considering the resale value where the EV Part stands for Extreme losses Value? The cost for parts is more expensive but the need for parts less. Seems the required maintenance is higher with an EV but I am not positive. Can we get a from new through average years of ownership to resale value sold with gas and electricity and installed charger costs or electric cost at fast charging not cheap overnight charging? You might be surprised to hear that this car is NOT a plug-in hybrid. Therefore, there is NO electricity cost! The high voltage battery in a non-plug-in hybrid is charged by regenerative braking and the actions of the hybrid system, including managing the CVT. Ultimately, the electricity comes from the gasoline that is burned by the engine. Wait, wait: you had a Subaru Forester??
Tell us more!! Of course the Honda is a better experience, especially in the “back to the dealer” department. Should have picked one instead of the Subaru in the first place, and you’d probably still be driving it. We have owned three Subaru vehicles and they have been fine. We moved from the midwest to AZ so ground clearance and AWD are no longer a priority, but where else can we get a station wagon? That’s what’s so frustrating… if you want a wagon, you basically have to get a lifted AWD vehicle or a fancy German one. One thing I hate about MPG as a measure of efficiency is it doesn’t scale well in real world use and past about 30-35MPG the big number looking improvements are pretty insignificant.  Here’s how many gallons it would take to drive 1000 miles in 5 MPG increments: 10MPG = 100G
15MPG = 66.7G
20MPG = 50G
25MPG = 40G
30MPG = 33.3G
35MPG = 28.6G
40MPG = 25G
45MPG = 22.2G
50MPG = 20G By simply switching from a 10MPG vehicle to a 15MPG vehicle you’ve saved more fuel on that one trip than someone else switching from a 20MPG vehicle to a 50MPG vehicle.  That 30MPG improvement between 20 and 50 sure does sound a lot more impressive than the 5MPG improvement between 10 and 15, but it actually accomplishes less. and I even made it to 35 without having to use a calculator! As someone with an 8MPG F250 in the fleet all I can say is… *sigh*.  (And yes I’m excited that the Telo is rated to tow 8000#) Exactly! I keep banging on about this too. Thinking of how many gallons per 1000 miles really puts things into perspective. Two mpg doesn’t sound like much at 10 mpg but it’s saving or using quite a bit of fuel. Thus the EU reporting fuel economy in l/100km.  Same result as your math above. The CVT was underwhelming in the way most CVTs from that era are… That’s not surprising. In my experience it’s necessary to go at least as far back as the early 1980s to find a car with a proper CVT. Getting 2 or 3 MPG more in the hybrid wouldn’t make sense cost wise. I’ve been sniffing around CRVs lately and found your comment very interesting. You’re dealing with a lot less complexity too. title: Texas v. Kennedy Update - Autistic Self Advocacy Network
content: The Department of Justice is a part of the government that makes sure laws are followed. We call it DOJ for short. The DOJ and a few states made another bad decision. This update talks about what they did. And we will talk about what the bad decision means for you. On August 31st, the DOJ and a few states asked a court to resolve an important lawsuit. To resolve a lawsuit means stopping the lawsuit. It also means the people suing each other agree to do things. The lawsuit the DOJ asked to resolve is called Texas v. Kennedy. Texas v. Kennedy is a lawsuit about Section 504 rules from Health and Human Services. Health and Human Services is the part of the U.S. government in charge of healthcare. We call it HHS for short. Section 504 is a part of a law from 1973. We call it 504 for short. 504 says places that get money from the government can’t discriminate against people with disabilities. Discrimination is treating people unfairly or badly because of who they are. Section 504 has rules for how the law should be followed. The DOJ decided the U.S. government should change part of these rules. These rules were made by HHS in 2024. This statement calls these rules the 2024 HHS 504 Rules. The 2024 HHS 504 Rules do a lot of important things. One of those things is updating the first 504 rules. Those rules are from 1978. This was the first time HHS updated the 504 rules since 1978. One of the most important things the 2024 HHS 504 Rules talked about is the integration mandate. The integration mandate is a rule that says people with disabilities have a right to live, work, and get services in the community. The 2024 HHS 504 Rules did not create the integration mandate. But the 2024 HHS 504 Rules said the integration mandate was a part of 504. Adding the integration mandate to the 504 rules makes the law stronger. The reason Section 504 got made was to stop discrimination against people with disabilities. Adding the integration mandate to the 504 rules would help stop discrimination that keeps disabled people out of the community. But the DOJ decided HHS will take away words talking about the integration mandate in the 2024 HHS 504 rules. This is bad. It is important that the 2024 HHS 504 rules have the integration mandate in them. But the DOJ and states did not take away the integration mandate. Taking away words about it in the 2024 HHS 504 rules does not take away the integration mandate. That is because the integration mandate does not come from HHS rules. The integration mandate is the law. The integration mandate comes from 504 and the Americans with Disabilities Act. The Americans with Disabilities Act is like 504. It is a law that protects people with disabilities from discrimination. We call it the ADA for short. The Supreme Court also agrees that the integration mandate is the law. The Supreme Court is the highest court in the United States. They have the final say on laws for the whole country. The Supreme Court said that the integration mandate is part of the ADA and 504. They did this in a court case in 1999 called Olmstead v. LC. We call this court case Olmstead for short. Olmstead says that people with disabilities had the right to live, work, and get services in the community. Olmstead says that the integration mandate is part of the ADA and 504. Olmstead, the ADA, 504, and the integration mandate are all still here. Your state still has to follow the integration mandate. States are not allowed to ignore the integration mandate. States that do not follow the integration mandate are breaking the law. The U.S. government still has to make sure your state follows the integration mandate. Making sure states follow the integration mandate is still their job. We deserve a government that protects our rights. We do not deserve a government that ignores our rights. ASAN demands states continue to follow the integration mandate.

title: Norway bids final farewell to popular King Harald V as crowds and royals converge for his funeral - KSL.com
content: OSLO, Norway — Norway bade its final farewell to Harald V on Wednesday as crowds lined the streets and foreign royals and leaders converged on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king, who was remembered as a popular monarch with a down-to-earth touch. A 21-gun salute rang out over the capital at the start of a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral. Harald's son, new King Haakon VIII, and other senior royals walked behind the coffin, draped with the red Norwegian royal standard. Harald's widow, Queen Sonja, and Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, followed in a car. Norwegian officials and foreign dignitaries joined the solemn procession. They included the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Jordan. Also present were the heir to the British throne, Prince William, and Japan's Crown Prince Akishino, as well as political leaders from more than 20 countries, including Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As the funeral service began, Norway came to a halt for a minute of silence. Harald, who died on Aug. 28 aged 89, was Europe's oldest monarch and had reigned for 35 years. He modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who recently abdicated. His son immediately became king and last week took an oath of allegiance to Norway's constitution in parliament. The parliament's speaker, Masud Gharahkhani, said at the service that "King Harald was close to the people" and recalled that "he wasn't afraid to meet people in his rubber boots." He remembered Harald saying in his 2008 New Year's address: "I wish we would stop using the term 'the weakest in society.' In reality, some of these people are among the strongest of us all." "He lived up to his motto: He gave his all for Norway," Gharahkhani said. Large crowds flocked to Oslo for the funeral, and thousands stood behind barriers on streets lined with national flags. The downtown area was closed to vehicles and electric scooters, and police had instructed people not to bring bicycles, umbrellas or sharp objects. People tuned in across the country of about 5.6 million. Scores of churches, libraries, cultural centers and city halls made big screens available for the public to watch the funeral, public broadcaster NRK reported. The government said it wasn't an official holiday, but schools and workplaces could individually opt to let students and employees watch. Ahead of the funeral, Norwegians waited patiently to file past Harald's coffin in the chapel of the royal palace. The queue was seven hours long at one point over the weekend. Over 46,000 people visited the chapel during the week it lay in state. "The love between the people and King Harald has not ended — quite the contrary," said Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit, who led the funeral service, pointing to the tributes left outside the palace after his death. "The sea of flowers, along with the words and drawings that accompany them, speaks loudly and clearly of a heart so full that it overflows." After the funeral, Harald's coffin was taken in a smaller procession to Akershus Fortress, where the late king's predecessors are buried in the palace chapel. Haakon followed with the two other Scandinavian monarchs, King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden and King Frederik X of Denmark. Norway's monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. The Norwegian royal house has kinfolk in other European royal families. Harald and Haakon are related to both Britain's King Charles III and Spain's King Felipe VI: They're all descendants of the U.K.'s Queen Victoria, who reigned from 1837 until her death in 1901. Today, the throne's role is largely symbolic and power lies with the elected government and parliament, but the Norwegian royal family retains a role in promoting the wealthy Scandinavian nation around the world. content: OSLO: Norway bid farewell on Wednesday to King Harald V in a funeral reflecting his open and unifying nature, and attended by dignitaries including Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky and Britain’s Prince William. After a procession through the streets of Oslo packed with crowds and a funeral service at Oslo’s Lutheran cathedral, the king’s casket was transported to the Akershus Castle church where it was to be placed in the royal crypt. Until his death on August 28 at age 89, Harald was the oldest reigning monarch in Europe and hugely popular among Norwegians, despite the scandals that dogged his family toward the end of his reign. Some 48,000 people lined the streets for the procession, police said. “He was our rock,” Inger Elise Kolsto, a 63-year-old accountant, told AFP. Carried on an artillery carriage, the king’s casket, draped in the red royal banner, was transported along the city’s main avenue, followed on foot by his son and heir King Haakon VIII, members of his family, and dozens of other dignitaries. Only Harald’s widow, 89-year-old Queen Sonja, and the new Queen Mette-Marit, who underwent a lung transplant in June, followed the procession in a car. Among other guests were Scandinavia’s royal families, royal couples from Spain, Belgium and the Netherlands, the crown prince of Japan, the presidents of Finland and Germany, and the French and Thai prime ministers. title: State of Oregon v. Trump - Cato Institute
content: The Federal Circuit should affirm the decision of the Court of International Trade and declare the new round of tariffs to be illegal. Learn more about Cato’s Amicus Briefs Program. In February 2026, the Supreme Court invalidated the massive tariffs that President Trump attempted to impose under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). But that decision did not end Trump’s efforts to unilaterally impose onerous tariffs. Now the President has invoked Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 to purportedly impose 10 percent tariffs on imports from almost all US trading partners. Soon after these new tariffs were announced, two small businesses and a coalition of 24 state governments filed lawsuits in the US Court of International Trade (CIT) challenging their legality. In May, the CIT ruled that these new tariffs are illegal. Now the case has been appealed to the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. Cato and Professor Ilya Somin, our B. Kenneth Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies, have filed an amicus brief supporting the CIT’s decision; Somin previously served as co-counsel to the victorious plaintiffs in the IEEPA Supreme Court tariff case. We thank Daniel Wolff, Alexander Schaefer, and Joshua Claybourn of Crowell & Moring for assistance in drafting and filing the brief. In our brief, we explain why this sweeping imposition of tariffs is just as illegal as the previous one was, and for many of the same reasons. First, our brief explains why Section 122 simply cannot be used in the current circumstances. The statute only permits tariffs for up to 150 days in response to “fundamental international payments problems” that cause “large and serious United States balance-of-payments deficits” or “an imminent and significant depreciation of the dollar,” or that create a need to cooperate with other countries in addressing an “international balance-of-payments disequilibrium.” But these conditions are only possible under a fixed exchange rate system, such as the one the US formerly had under the gold standard. These conditions cannot and do not exist in a flexible exchange rate regime of the sort in place today. Next, we explain why, if there is any ambiguity about whether Section 122 authorizes the massive tariffs imposed by the administration, the major questions doctrine requires this issue to be resolved against the government. The major questions doctrine requires Congress to “speak clearly” when it assigns to the executive “decisions of vast economic and political significance.” The impact of the new Section 122 tariffs is as large or larger than many previous policies invalidated by the Supreme Court on major questions doctrine grounds. And the tariff power is not exempt from major questions scrutiny on the supposed ground that it is a “foreign affairs” power. The major questions doctrine also counts against giving the administration a blank check in determining whether the preconditions to invoke Section 122 exist. Finally, if the court were to conclude that Section 122 does somehow grant the president the sweeping power he claims, it must rule that the law is an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power to the executive. Congress cannot give the president what would essentially be unlimited power to impose up to 15% tariffs on imports from any nation, especially since the administration’s approach would allow the executive to circumvent the 150-day time limit simply by declaring that a new balance-of-payments crisis has arisen after it expires. The Federal Circuit should affirm the decision of the Court of International Trade and declare the new round of tariffs to be illegal. Professor of Law, George Mason University, and B. Kenneth Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies, Cato Institute Director, Robert A. content: Today, Wednesday, September 9th, the eyes of the world are on Oslo for the State Funeral of King Harald V of Norway, who passed away on August 28 at the age of 89 after several days in the hospital. Since then, the entire country has been mourning the loss of its beloved sovereign, regarded by several generations as the “grandfather of the nation.” Since Tuesday afternoon, numerous royals have arrived, among them King Felipe and Queen Letizia; Princess Alexia of Greece with her husband, Carlos Morlaes, her brother, Prince Nikolaos of Greece, and her mother, Queen Anne-Marie; Alois of Liechtenstein; Abdullah and Rania of Jordan; and Rosario Nadal, a close friend of Queen Mette-Marit. They were all seen around the Grand Hotel as they gathered for a historic reception hosted by Haakon VIII and Mette-Marit. King Harald’s coffin has arrived at Akershus Fortress, his final resting place. Located in the heart of Oslo overlooking the fjord, Akershus is one of Norway’s most important historic landmarks. Construction began around 1290, and over the centuries it evolved from a medieval castle into a fortress. For more than 700 years, Akershus has been closely tied to Norway’s monarchy and government, and today it is home to the royal mausoleum. Following King Harald’s funeral service, Crown Princess Victoria of Sweden and Princess Catharina-Amalia of the Netherlands were seen sharing a relaxed conversation. Both are future queens, although they belong to different generations of European royalty. One of the most poignant images of the day was King Haakon of Norway surrounded by King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden and King Frederik X of Denmark during the final procession before King Harald’s burial. The three Scandinavian monarchies share deep historical ties and decades of friendship. In a final tribute, Norwegian Armed Forces aircraft flew over Oslo before King Harald V’s coffin began its journey to his final resting place in the crypt at Akershus Castle. The procession continued to the sound of a funeral march performed by a military band. Following the funeral, King Harald’s coffin is being carried in procession to Akershus Castle Church, where a private ceremony will be held for the family and royal guests. The president of the Storting, Norway’s prime minister and the chief justice of the Supreme Court will also attend, along with the presidents of Iceland and Finland. The coffin will then be lowered into the crypt of the castle church, where King Haakon VII, Queen Maud, King Olav V and Crown Princess Märtha are also laid to rest. “We give thanks for King Harald and for all you have given us through his life” “Eternal God, our refuge in this time of sorrow, draw near to us with your peace. Strengthen us in faith. Give us a future and hope. We give thanks for King Harald and for all you have given us through his life. Merciful God, we commend him into your hands. You who created us in your image and gave us Jesus Christ as our Savior, raise us on the last day to eternal life with you,” the farewell prayer read. In one of the more emotional moments of the service, Princess Ingrid Alexandra offered support to her younger brother, Prince Sverre Magnus, during the performance of Abide with Me. “May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace.” Crown Princess Victoria of Sweden stepped forward to lead a prayer, first making a final curtsy to her godfather, King Harald. The future queen of Sweden then read the Prayer of St. Francis in Swedish. The prayer carries special significance for Victoria and the Norwegian royal family. She recited the same prayer when King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit married at Oslo Cathedral in 2001. The Swedish crown princess was also among the first royals to support the relationship of Norway’s now King and Queen. Music has played a central role throughout King Harald’s funeral, accompanying some of the most moving moments of the historic service. The ceremony was presided over by Presiding Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit and followed the funeral rites of the Church of Norway. Bishop of Oslo Sunniva Gylver also took part in the service. A passage from the Gospel of John was read in Sámi during the funeral service: “I am the good shepherd. I know my own and my own know me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one will take them out of my hand. What my Father has given me is greater than all else, and no one can take it out of the Father’s hand.” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre also paid tribute to Queen Sonja, highlighting her tireless dedication to culture, nature and traveling to even the most remote corners of Norway. “I have an image etched in my memory. At the top of Stortinden, in Vågan municipality in Lofoten, stands Dronningvarden, with the words ‘for a country.’ But I say, on behalf of all of us, for a queen.” The traditional song “Jørgen Hattemaker” was performed during the funeral service. The song tells the story of a hatmaker who compares his life with that of King Solomon. Despite the differences between them, both ultimately share the same fundamental condition as human beings. “We are deeply grateful for King Harald’s 35 years as King of Norway, but above all for the person he was. He brought humanity to the solemnity of the monarchy. When we were happy, he was happy with us, with laughter and a twinkle in his eye,” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. The President of the Norwegian Parliament delivers the first address during King Harald’s funeral service at Oslo Cathedral. The entire nation observes a minute of silence in honor of King Harald, beginning and ending with three tolls of the bell. The guests inside Oslo Cathedral then take their seats. All guests have now taken their seats inside Oslo Cathedral as King Harald’s funeral service begins. The King’s family is seated on one side of the altar, while members of royal families from around the world are seated on the other. A Royal Guard soldier fainted at Palace Square shortly before King Harald’s funeral procession began. The soldier lost consciousness and has since been evacuated. According to Norwegian news agency NTB, another soldier was also removed from formation at a different location. More than 200,000 people, including 53,000 in central Oslo, have taken part in King Harald’s state funeral, as Norway comes together for a historic and deeply solemn royal farewell. Upon their arrival at Oslo Cathedral, Queen Sonja, King Haakon and Queen Mette-Marit, Princess Märtha Louise, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus were welcomed by church officials. Other members of the royal families in attendance then began entering the cathedral. Princess Märtha Louise’s three daughters, Maud Angelica, Leah Isadora and Emma Tallulah, have entered Oslo Cathedral alongside Durek Verrett and Marius Borg Høiby. King Harald’s funeral procession is approaching Oslo Cathedral as thousands of Norwegians line the streets, respectfully paying their final tribute to the late monarch. A profound silence has fallen over Oslo as King Harald’s funeral procession makes its way through the city. Alongside the Norwegian royal family, members of royal families from across Europe have joined this solemn moment, including King Felipe and Queen Letizia of Spain, King Willem-Alexander and Queen Máxima of the Netherlands, and their daughter, Princess Catharina-Amalia. King Haakon, accompanied by his children, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus, and his sister, Princess Märtha Louise, escorts King Harald’s coffin during his final journey through the crowded streets of Oslo. Queens Mette-Marit and Sonja follow in a car behind them. King Harald’s coffin has left the chapel at the Royal Palace, where members of his family and dozens of Norwegians paid their respects, and is now making its way to Oslo Cathedral for the funeral service. Draped in the royal standard and topped with a wreath of flowers, the coffin has been placed on a purple velvet catafalque. Prince Albert and Princess Charlene of Monaco were seen boarding the bus that will take them to Oslo Cathedral for King Harald V’s state funeral. The Grimaldi flag is also flying at half-staff in Monaco as a sign of mourning following the Norwegian monarch’s death. Queen Rania of Jordan was also seen leaving the Grand Hotel in the Norwegian capital, following the royal protocol and dress code for the solemn occasion. Grand Duchess Maria Teresa shared a heartfelt tribute ahead of the funeral: “On this day of the funeral of the much-loved King of Norway, I remember with emotion the immense affection he always showed me. I will never forget his wonderful sense of humor either.” Dressed in military uniform, King Frederik X left the Danish royal yacht alongside his wife, Queen Mary, as the couple made their way to King Harald’s funeral. The Danish royals chose to travel to Oslo aboard their own vessel and spend the night there rather than stay at a hotel. Marius Borg Høiby, who is serving a four-year sentence from Skaugum Palace, was seen leaving by car as part of a motorcade that also included his mother, Queen Mette-Marit, King Haakon VIII, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus. As Harald V’s coffin is carried through the streets of Oslo to his final resting place, every branch of the Armed Forces will be represented to render him their last honors. A total of 1,900 service members from all the services will line the route along the streets. The United Kingdom, Sweden, and Denmark have also sent troops. In addition to being closed to traffic, downtown Oslo has been equipped with giant screens so people can follow all of today’s events. More than 170 churches across the country will also broadcast the funeral ceremony live. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium and the Grand Duke and Grand Duchess of Luxembourg, Guillaume and Stéphanie, have arrived together by bus. The monarchs are dressed in their full ceremonial uniforms and decorations. The Swedish Royal Family has already landed in Oslo. It is one of the monarchies sending the largest delegation to this State Funeral, due to strong family and friendship ties. Crown Princess Victoria is one of King Harald’s godchildren and one of those who has most deeply mourned the loss of her “dear” godfather. In addition, King Carl Gustaf has already announced that on Wednesday there will be a bell-ringing ceremony at Riddarholm Church in Stockholm. Harald V was appointed Knight of the Royal Order of the Seraphim by King Gustaf VI Adolf in 1958. In 1992, he received the chain of this Order. Before 9:00 a.m., King Felipe VI’s standard was lowered to half-mast at the Royal Palace in Madrid as a sign of mourning on the day of King Harald V of Norway’s funeral. At the moment of his interment, it will be raised to the top of the mast in tribute to King Haakon VIII. Despite his recent kidney transplant, Durek Verrett arrived at the Royal Palace with his wife, Princess Märtha Louise of Norway, to join the Norwegian Royal Family in their grief and in this major tribute to King Harald. Princess Märtha Louise is no longer an active member of the Royal Family, but she always maintained a very close and loving relationship with her father. King Harald and Queen Sonja attended their daughter’s wedding to the shaman to the Hollywood stars. Very early on Wednesday morning, at 7:00 a.m., Queen Sonja was seen out for a walk in sportswear through the Royal Palace park. Cell phone in hand, she took a photo of her own statue, which was covered in flowers. Today will be an incredibly difficult day for her: she will say a final goodbye to the man she was married to for almost 58 years and with whom she shared a royal love story unlike any other. Oslo has gone into maximum security mode for an event that has posed a major security and logistical challenge. Flights have been canceled at the airport so that planes carrying royals and dignitaries from around the world can land to say farewell to the Nordic monarch. © ¡HOLA! title: Gillings MCH center hosts national gathering to build Title V skills - sph.unc.edu
content:
In order to improve the health of women, children and families, it’s essential that state agencies partner with other organizations to increase the impact of their Title V Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Services Block Grant funding. Equally essential is that they partner strategically, selecting the right partners and building collaborations that are mutually beneficial, effective, and sustainable. Map of the states and jurisdictions that sent Title V teams to the skills institute: Alabama, American Samoa, Colorado, Guam, Hawai‘i, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Minnesota, North Carolina, North Dakota, the Northern Mariana Islands, Mississippi, Pennsylvania, Puerto Rico, South Dakota, Tennessee, Virginia, and Washington, and Wisconsin. In early August, the National MCH Workforce Development Center, part of the UNC Gillings School of Global Public Health’s MCH department, hosted a three-day skills institute in Tempe, Arizona, to help Title V professionals strengthen their skills in strategic partnership. The event, titled “Grow Your Title V Impact through Strategic Partnerships,” brought together 86 MCH professionals, representing 21 state and jurisdictional teams. Over the three days, Center experts presented a series of workshops, introducing tools that each team could use to assess their readiness and capacity for partnership, build strategic and mutually beneficial partnerships, assess and learn from partnership efforts, and build sustainability into their partnerships. The skills institute participants with Center staff. The workshops included presentations from Title V professionals in Arizona, Minnesota, North Carolina and Virginia who reflected on their own efforts to take a strategic approach to partnership. After each workshop, the teams worked in breakout rooms with Center coaches to apply the workshop’s tools to their own unique contexts. In their evaluation, a participant shared that the skills institute “struck the right balance between case study speakers, tool introductions and time for applying those tools with our team. It went beyond getting inspired and into taking action, which helps form the pathways for us to continue our work when we return home.” Some teams came to the skills institute with only Title V professionals, so they could use the tools presented to think critically about who they should partner with and how to build or strengthen those partnerships for the greatest impact. Other teams included representatives from partner organizations, so Title V staff could work directly with their partners to apply the tools to the work they are tackling together. The Puerto Rico team used “Balance of Petals,” a systems thinking tool, to identify other partners they should bring into their work and assess how mutually beneficial their existing and potential partnerships can be. For example, a team from Puerto Rico included three Title V professionals and two representatives from different partner organizations. With a March of Dimes representative, they discussed how to improve compliance with a regulation that requires “hard stop” policies at birthing hospitals, which aim to prevent complications for mothers and babies by reducing labor inductions before 39 weeks unless medically necessary. With a leader from the Puerto Rico Institute on Developmental Disabilities, they discussed how to improve developmental screening rates so that children with autism can be identified earlier and receive services and support sooner. By attending the skills institute together with partners, the team was able to gain clarity about the goals of both change initiatives and what roles would be best for each partner. They also identified other partners who would be important to add to their efforts, discussed their perceptions of how mutually beneficial the partnerships were, and built 30-, 60- and 90-day action plans for moving their work forward. “As always, we were grateful for the opportunity to work in person with MCH professionals from across the country,” said Rebecca Greenleaf, MPH, the director of learning for the National MCH Workforce Development Center, who led the development of the skills institute’s curriculum. “It’s exciting to create a space where our staff and MCH professionals working in the field can learn from each other. We look forward to integrating what we learned at this event into our Center’s future offerings.” Read the full story from the National MCH Workforce Development Center. title: King Felipe VI’s uniform at Harald V’s funeral: Every symbol explained - HOLA
content: King Felipe VI arrived in Oslo on Wednesday to bid farewell to Norway’s King Harald V at his state funeral, accompanied by Queen Letizia and Queen Sofía. For the solemn occasion, the Spanish monarch wore the Navy’s full-dress uniform reserved for his rank as Captain General, complete with medals, insignia and deeply symbolic details. One detail in particular stands out: the red Captain General’s sash around Felipe VI’s waist, presented to him by his father, King Juan Carlos, on the day he became King. The historic piece dates back to June 19, 2014, when Juan Carlos personally placed it on his son shortly before Felipe was proclaimed King and assumed supreme command of Spain’s Armed Forces. It wasn’t the only meaningful decoration he wore in Oslo. His uniform also included a special tribute to Norway. The first question raised by the images is exactly which uniform the King chose for the occasion. The answer can be found in Spain’s Armed Forces uniform regulations. Felipe VI is wearing the Spanish Navy’s full-dress uniform, rather than its most formal ceremonial version. Order DEF/114/2025 establishes that the full-dress uniform is worn, among other solemn occasions, at the burials and funerals of heads of state. His choice for Harald V’s funeral therefore follows military protocol. In the Navy, this uniform consists of a navy-blue frock coat, a white shirt, a black tie, full-size decorations, white gloves and, for general officers, a red sash. In the King’s case, however, there is another distinction. This is not simply a Spanish Navy full-dress uniform. It is the uniform he wears as Captain General, the highest military rank he holds as Spain’s head of state. The most striking element of Felipe VI’s uniform is the red sash around his waist, a piece with profound historical significance. King Juan Carlos presented it to his son on the morning of June 19, 2014, at Zarzuela Palace, shortly before Felipe VI swore allegiance to the Constitution and was proclaimed King before the Spanish Parliament. The gesture symbolized the transfer of supreme command of the Armed Forces to the new monarch. Since then, the sash has become one of the defining elements of the King’s appearances in military uniform as Captain General of the Armed Forces. Article 62 of the Spanish Constitution states that the King holds “supreme command of the Armed Forces,” one of the constitutional responsibilities associated with the Crown. The sash’s color is no coincidence. Red is the traditional color of the Spanish military sash, a custom dating back to the era of the Spanish Tercios that has remained associated with generals and the military’s highest-ranking officers. The sash is worn around the waist over the tunic or frock coat and tied in a bow on the left side. Its two ends hang from the bow and are finished with large gold tassels. The sash also features what are known in Spanish military terminology as entorchados, embroidered chains of leaves that identify general officers. The number of these embroidered elements corresponds to the four-pointed stars associated with military rank. In Felipe VI’s case, as Captain General, there are five stars, denoting the highest rank. What at first glance might look like a simple red sash is therefore one of the pieces that most clearly illustrates the King’s constitutional and military role. Another of the most important distinctions in Felipe VI’s life can be seen on his chest: the Order of the Golden Fleece. The then Prince of Asturias received the prestigious honor from King Juan Carlos in 1981, when he was just 13 years old. It has a particularly strong connection to his personal history, having accompanied the current King throughout much of his time as heir to the throne. More than four decades later, the Golden Fleece once again appears on his uniform during an occasion of extraordinary solemnity, with Felipe VI representing Spain alongside members of Europe’s other royal families. Another red sash visible in the images could easily cause some confusion. Felipe VI is also wearing the Grand Cross of the Royal Norwegian Order of St. Olav, one of Norway’s highest honors. The sash, worn diagonally across his chest, takes on particular significance in Oslo. Felipe VI received the distinction while he was still Prince of Asturias, and wearing it at Harald V’s funeral serves as a gesture of respect toward both the Norwegian royal family and a nation Spain joins in mourning today. The corresponding star of the order can also be seen alongside the other decorations on the King’s uniform. Felipe VI’s uniform also displays several of his other major honors. Among them is the Grand Cross of the Royal and Distinguished Spanish Order of Charles III, one of Spain’s highest civil orders. Also prominent are the three Grand Crosses representing the country’s three branches of the Armed Forces: Military Merit, Naval Merit and Aeronautical Merit. The presence of all three decorations carries a clear significance. Felipe VI is Captain General of all three branches and, as King, holds supreme command of Spain’s Armed Forces. This is where one of the details most clearly connects Felipe VI’s appearance with that of his daughter. Princess Leonor has gradually added the same three military Grand Crosses to her uniform as she has completed the different stages of her military training. The heir to the throne first received the Grand Cross of Military Merit, followed by the Grand Cross of Naval Merit and, finally, the Grand Cross of Aeronautical Merit. Together, they form the same trio of decorations worn by her father. The parallel is no coincidence. Leonor is following the military path expected of the future monarch, who will one day be called upon to serve as Captain General of the Armed Forces, a role the Constitution assigns to the sovereign. Two final details complete Felipe VI’s appearance in Oslo: the white gloves and the peaked cap he wears on his head. White gloves are a regulation component of the full-dress uniform and add an additional degree of formality to attire reserved for ceremonies of particular importance. In photographs from the funeral, the King can be seen holding them in his hand as he greets officials and other attendees. He also wears the Spanish Navy’s peaked cap, with a black visor and the insignia corresponding to his rank. It is another element of the uniform that identifies his status as Captain General of the Navy and of Spain’s Armed Forces as a whole. © ¡HOLA! title: There’s Something About Sarah - The Bulwark
content: I want to kvell about my best friend today. Thank you for your indulgence. Last night Sarah and I did a show at the famous 92nd Street Y in New York. We were there to celebrate her book, How to Eat an Elephant, which I’m sure you’ve already ordered. But if not, go ahead and do it now. I’m so proud of her. Proud that she did the book. Proud that she wrote it herself instead of using a ghost. Proud of how it turned out. But while the book is the impetus, I mostly just want to tell you why I love Sarah. We have a lot of new readers and I’m not sure how many of you know the origin of our friendship, so here’s the quick-sketch version. For fifteen years Sarah and I worked two blocks away from each other in Washington, D.C., and shared many of the same friends. Despite this, we never met. Or even knew about each other’s existence. When The Weekly Standard, the magazine where I spent my entire adult life, was shut down in 2018 I scrambled to find jobs for my team. I called in every favor. One of my friends (Sonny) told me to call Sarah Longwell. I cold-called her from the parking lot of a strip-center Starbucks. Told her that she didn’t know me, but I’d been sent her way by our mutual friend. I told her that I needed help. That I needed to find jobs for my talented colleagues who were about to get royally fucked by our idiot billionaire owner. Within minutes she was taking down names, job descriptions, and salary requirements. She said she’d call me back in hour. Sarah came through and found jobs for five of the people on my team. She decided she was going to turn TheBulwark.com from a link aggregator into a media property. This was something I’d done before, so she asked me to help. I said I’d be happy to, but that I wouldn’t stay long-term. I was getting out of journalism. So while Sarah and I and the OG Bulwark team were incepting This Thing of Ours, I was out interviewing with various tech companies.1 But we kept building and The Bulwark kept growing and when it came to making a decision—jump into a tech gig or stay at The Bulwark—I didn’t want to leave. We initially built The Bulwark as a nonprofit. Why? Because in the history of political magazines, there were only two economic models. You could be a successful nonprofit supported by donations, or a failing for-profit supported by a wealthy owner who didn’t mind losing money. No political magazines made money. Not ever. It was an impossible dream. When we launched Bulwark+ the idea was to bring in small-dollar donors alongside our big, institutional donors. But things got out of hand, fast. When we launched Bulwark+, my stretch goal was 10,000 members by the end of year one. I thought we got lucky and should sit tight and count our blessings. Sarah wanted to push forward. She came up with a plan to take us for-profit and grow even bigger. Much bigger. A bigger audience would mean more influence in the public debate. More resources would allow us to bring in new voices to fight alongside us. It’s important to note that at the time, The Bulwark was still something of a side project for Sarah. She had recently started her own communications firm, which was already more than a full-time job. That was a stable, steady business; I worried that the effort of turning The Bulwark into a for-profit venture would be a tremendous drain. I begged her not to. I told her that the media industry was dying and corporate comms was an honorable, reliable profession. We argued about it for weeks; I was dead set against Sarah’s idea. The last time we argued about it, I tried to impress on Sarah, again, how risky her plan was. We were both parents with young kids. We had obligations to take care of our families. She needed to protect her career options going forward. “I’m in this up to my eyeballs already, JVL,” she said. “I have to fight this fight.” She said that if I wanted to keep The Bulwark as a nonprofit, she could find a way to do that. But that she would go out and start something else, because she believed in this mission. Because I realized that I never wanted to work without Sarah again. I wanted to spend the rest of my career in the trenches next to her. Sarah is ambitious, but not in the Washington sense of the word. She’s relentlessly energetic. Always moving. Always hustling. But she isn’t motivated by vanity. What keeps her motor running is a simple desire. And I’m going to share it with you, because it’s the key to understanding everything about her. I am not like that. I have entire classes of people I would like to load onto a Falcon Heavy and launch straight into the sun. Not Sarah. When she watches people, she looks for their best selves. She’s patient with their shortcomings; empathetic about their struggles. She’s not a Pollyanna, but she’s an optimist. She believes that the future can be better and that we can all make it through this life, if we work together and show grace. She has a commitment to human dignity that is rare outside the communion of saints. As you know, Sarah and I have many disagreements. Just as a for-instance, our policy preferences don’t align perfectly. On subjects where we do align, we often have different prudential judgments about the best way to get from here to there. And we operate from two different views concerning the overall state of play in America. I think we’re right fucked. That the American age is over and we are at the beginning of a period of decline that might be arrested temporarily, but is ultimately inexorable. Sarah thinks that we can build back better. That from this crucible can emerge a more perfect union. That there is no fate but what we make. That’s what her book is about. It’s both a call to arms and a battle plan. She’s taken eight years of focus groups and built a theory of how to beat the fascists. It’s smart. It’s practical. It’s deeply courageous. I don’t share Sarah’s hope. Like I said: I think we’re cooked. But that’s on the analysis side. On the question of what we do, practically, right now, together, in this fight? I roll how Sarah rolls. Whether we save America or go down swinging, I’m with her. And the two of us are with you guys. Ride or die, fam. Thank you for building this thing with us. Thank you for supporting my best friend. Funny story: There was an early edition of the Triad in which I accidentally included a link to my résumé. I’m glad JVL didn’t end up as a middle manager for Meta. VERY glad. The moment I fell for Sarah hook, line and sinker was a Next Level where Tim or JVL made a reference to bukkake and Sarah genuinely had no idea what they were talking about. Such a savvy and fierce political operative and yet so genuinely unsullied by our very sullied age. A happy warrior, that's our Sarah! Emergency Triad: The United States commits imperial suicide. content: Currently, only residents from GDPR countries and certain US states can opt out of Tracking Technologies through our Consent Management Platform.
