People are not happy about Flock Safety’s automated license plate readers and the cops that allegedly misuse them. If you’re one of those ALPR-haters, you can now take out your rage in the video game Grand Theft Auto V by installing Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, a mod built by artist Morry Kolman. The mod installs 235 Flock cameras around the fictional Los Santos, a riff on the real-life city of Los Angeles. Players can smash and shoot down the cameras and get paid $600 for each one they destroy, which Kolman priced based on a teardown of a Flock Falcon Flex Camera by the Iowa-based civil liberties group Eyes Off of Cedar Rapids. The in-game cameras log every time a player destroys and drives by one, and players can render a photo album of their interactions. In real life, vigilantes have allegedly wrecked Flock cameras in their communities using spray-paint, saws, bullets, and even flaming projectiles. An NPR analysis found that Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states. “GTPLR is not an endorsement of the activities that it allows in the game in the same way that GTA is not an endorsement of the activities that are allowed in the game,” says Kolman, referring to the fact that GTA is largely about doing fictional crimes. “But I think there is a public appetite for some kind of cathartic release against these machines.” In addition to being fun objects to destroy, the GTA cameras also operate as an extension of the police in-game. Passing by one of the 235 cameras while being chased by the cops prolongs the game’s cooldown period. Because of how dense the cameras are in some areas, it can make the game impossible to play. There’s also a 5 percent chance that the cameras will trigger a random police response even if the player isn’t doing anything wrong, which Kolman says was inspired by news reports about innocent people being held at gunpoint because of ALPR errors. “There are violent responses and really dangerous situations that are created by these cameras and their inaccuracies,” says Kolman. Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment for this story. GTA V has been around for over a decade, and a rich modding community has built up around it (WIRED covered one back in 2015.) The long-awaited sequel, Grand Theft Auto VI, is slated to come out in November and will be set in a fictional version of Miami called Vice City. Kolman doesn’t have specific plans to build a version of GTALPR for that, joking, “We'll probably wait to see what the people of Vice City and their local government have already installed around their map.” In real-life LA, the Los Angeles Police Department suspended its use of Flock cameras this summer following a recommendation from the LAPD’s inspector general. The tide is turning in other places too—governors in both Texas and Florida recently took steps to curtail the use of Flock cameras in their respective states, and across the US, there were 131 Flock contract terminations in August alone, according to the anti-surveillance advocacy group Secure Justice. For all the fun that fake-smashing surveillance cameras can be, Kolman seriously hopes that players can feel the “insidiousness and inescapability of the surveillance” through GTALPR. “I know that you could read a thousand articles about why surveillance is bad and why Flock is horrible,” says Kolman. “Or I could make you feel how pervasive these Flock cameras are by having you try to drive around the map of Los Santos.” Be the first to start the conversation! title: An Elegant Royal Farewell to King Harald V of Norway in Oslo - The Court Jeweller
content: Don’t Miss a Single Sparkling Moment! Sign up for The Court Jeweller Newsletter The extended royal family gathered in the Norwegian capital today to bid farewell to King Harald V of Norway in a state funeral service held at Oslo Cathedral. King Haakon VIII of Norway led the mourners today at the funeral for his late father, King Harald V, in Oslo. The late monarch’s coffin was transported from the Royal Palace to Oslo Cathedral in a solemn procession. King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, Prince Sverre Magnus, and Princess Märtha Louise walked behind the coffin. In a remarkable sight for the modern era, the procession also included numerous other royals, including the sovereigns of Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands, Jordan, Spain, Luxembourg, and Monaco, and the heirs of the United Kingdom, Japan, and Liechtenstein. Nearly all of the royal ladies in attendance wore the expected mourning attire: black with pearls. Here, Queen Sonja of Norway arrives with her son, King Haakon VIII, for the service. She also pinned her late husband’s Royal Family Order to her dress. Queen Mette-Marit also wore the late King’s Royal Family Order, plus pearl and diamond cluster earrings and a three-row pearl necklace. Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra wore King Harald’s Royal Family Order with a special necklace. The heart-shaped pendant, suspended from a single row of pearls, is set with diamonds and a central ruby, reflecting Norway’s national colors. The necklace was given to Ingrid Alexandra by her grandmother, Queen Sonja, as a christening present in 2004. Princess Märtha Louise arrived for her father’s funeral wearing his Royal Family Order and pearls, including a lovely five-row choker necklace with an antique diamond and pearl clasp. King Harald’s sister, Princess Astrid, wore pearls as well, plus the Royal Family Orders of her brother, their father (King Olav V), and their grandfather (King Haakon VII). The deep family and diplomatic ties between the late King and heads of state around the world were reflected in the guest list for the funeral. The entire Swedish royal family was in attendance: King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia (who wore pearls with an antique diamond bow brooch), Crown Princess Victoria and Prince Daniel, Prince Carl Philip and Princess Sofia, Princess Madeleine and Chris O’Neill, and Princess Christina and Tord Magnuson. King Harald was Crown Princess Victoria’s godfather, and she read a prayer during the funeral service. She wore pearl earrings, a pearl necklace with a cluster clasp, and a lovely antique heart-shaped mourning brooch. Sarah Williams has confirmed that the brooch was a gift to Victoria from King Harald. Princess Sofia and Princess Madeleine wore minimal jewelry: a little cluster brooch on Sofia’s coat, and small stud earrings for Madeleine. Denmark was represented by King Frederik X, Queen Mary, and Crown Prince Christian, plus Princess Benedikte with Princess Alexandra of Sayn-Wittgenstein-Berleburg. (Queen Margrethe was scheduled to attend but had to cancel following a recent hospitalization.) Mary wore pearl and diamond earrings and a pearl and diamond cluster brooch from a suite of jewels that belonged to Queen Lovisa of Denmark, King Harald’s great-grandmother. The Greek royal branch of the Danish royal family was also well-represented, with Queen Anne-Marie, Crown Prince Pavlos, Prince Nikolaos, Princess Alexia, and Carlos Morales Quintana also in attendance at the service. Queen Anne-Marie wore a golden flower brooch for the occasion. The Belgian royals and Norwegian royals are close cousins—King Harald’s mother, Crown Princess Märtha, and King Philippe’s grandmother, Queen Astrid, were sisters. For the funeral, Queen Mathilde wore a pearl choker, her diamond butterfly brooch, and Queen Fabiola’s pearl drop earrings. She wore the same combination of jewels for the funeral of Queen Elizabeth II four years ago. The Luxembourgish royals are also close cousins, as Grand Duke Guillaume V is a great-grandson of Queen Astrid. He attended alongside his wife, Grand Duchess Stéphanie, who wore earrings set with dark gemstones, and his father, Grand Duke Henri. The Dutch royal family was represented by King Willem-Alexander, Queen Máxima, Princess Amalia, and Princess Beatrix. Máxima wore pearl earrings with a nineteenth-century pearl and diamond brooch from the family collection. Máxima also wore this brooch for Queen Elizabeth II’s state funeral in 2022. Princess Amalia borrowed pearl and diamond earrings from her mother’s collection for the occasion. She also wore a pearl ring. Amalia sat beside her grandmother, Princess Beatrix, during the service. Beatrix wore more pearl jewelry, including a bangle bracelet with pearl tips. Queen Letizia of Spain wore her Ansorena diamond and pearl drop earrings for the service, plus a special necklace. The strand of pearls is part of Queen Ena’s joyas de pasar collection, which is earmarked for the use of the Queen of Spain. Queen Sofia wore pearls, too, though photos of her weren’t plentiful. Here, you catch a glimpse of her as she greets the Prince of Wales, the grandson of her Greek royal cousin, Prince Philip. The King and Queen of Jordan were present as well. Queen Rania does not usually wear much traditional jewelry for these kinds of mourning events, and today was no exception. Also in minimal jewelry—pearl stud earrings and her diamond engagement ring—was Princess Charlene of Monaco, who attended with her husband, Prince Albert II. Hereditary Princess Sophie of Liechtenstein brought along pearl and diamond pieces for the service, including a two-row pearl necklace and a lovely diamond ribbon brooch. We saw her wear the same brooch at Queen Elizabeth II’s funeral in 2022. The Emperor and Empress of Japan were represented by Crown Prince Fumihito and Crown Princess Kiko, who wore black earrings and a matching beaded necklace, plus a luminous dark bow brooch. Prince William represented his father at the funeral, but there was also another British royal family member in attendance: the Princess Royal, who wore her gold and diamond ribbon brooch for the service. Anne was present in a personal capacity; she is King Haakon’s godmother. The former monarchy of Serbia was represented by Crown Prince Alexander, who has remained close to his Scandinavian cousins over the years. He was joined by Crown Princess Katherine, who wore a gold ring on her right hand. After the funeral, the King’s body was interred in the Royal Mausoleum at Akershus Castle, beside his parents and his grandparents. The royals returned to the Royal Palace, where they held an official reception for their guests. King Haakon VIII, Queen Mette-Marit, Queen Sonja, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Prince Sverre Magnus also made a brief appearance on the palace balcony, waving in gratitude to the thousands of mourners gathered below. This story is taken from the autumn 2026 issue of Dazed, which is on sale internationally from September 10. Pre-order a copy of the magazine here. Everywhere V goes, he is accompanied by screams. Whether he’s attending a fashion show, performing at a sold-out arena or even making the short trip from his blacked-out SUV to the foyer of a five-star hotel, the BTS star’s life is soundtracked by an unbroken chorus of ear-splitting shrieks. When I meet him away from the crowds, in a nondescript studio in central Paris, the contrast between this mania and his calm, gentle demeanour is stark. In person, V is softly spoken, flawlessly polite and has a cheeky, slightly goofy sense of humour. Together, these qualities make for an endearing combination. Excluding the photoshoot, we are granted just two short audiences with him; both conversations are strictly off the record. (Although I can confirm that he essentially just introduced himself, asked if I’d been to Korea, said he could recommend some restaurants for the next time I was in Seoul, and thanked us for having him on the cover of the magazine.) The scale of V’s success, along with his bandmates j-hope, Jimin, Jin, Jung Kook, RM and Suga, is difficult to comprehend. In 2024, BTS became the most-streamed band of all time on Spotify, becoming the first to surpass 100bn streams across all platforms with the release of their tenth album, ARIRANG, in March this year. Along with the Beatles, they are one of only two groups in history to score three number one albums on the US Billboard chart in a single year. In fact, in terms of cultural impact, the Beatles are the only band that offers a meaningful comparison. One in 13 tourists to South Korea cites BTS as their main reason for visiting, and the group contributes an estimated US$4.65bn to the Korean economy each year. V is the soulful “fashion diva” (his stylist’s words) of the group, known for his rich baritone voice and retro, romantic style (see: his preference for louche tailoring and Michael Rider’s Celine). He reached a million followers on Instagram within 43 minutes of opening his account in 2021 – a Guinness World Record feat – and is now, with 75 million fans and counting, the most followed male K-pop artist on the platform. This is all to say that V is one of the most formidable forces in contemporary pop. But what do we know about the man himself? Well, at the age of 30, he’s recently completed 18 months of active service in the South Korean army, serving in an elite counter-terrorism unit under the military police. He was born on December 30, 1995, in Daegu, the fourth-largest city in South Korea, and was raised largely by his paternal grandparents while his parents worked. He debuted with BTS when he was just 17, after accompanying a friend to an audition where he was spotted by recruiters. After more than a decade with the band, he launched his solo career with his debut EP, Layover, in September 2023. He’s a Capricorn sun, an Aries moon and (according to BTS fan sites) a Sagittarius rising. He loves animals and had a black-and-tan pomeranian called Yeontan, who sadly died in 2024. He likes jazz, photography, art and fashion; Bing Crosby, Louis Armstrong, Kurt Cobain and John Legend. And despite channelling some of these musicians into his cool-guy-in-a-smoky-club aesthetic, he doesn’t take himself too seriously – as evidenced by his unfiltered chats with fans on Weverse, the general buffoonery of Run BTS, and his willingness to eat a series of increasingly spicy chicken wings on YouTube. The stage feels like V’s natural habitat. He performs with such ease, such deftness, that it’s clear this is what he was born – and trained – to do. At a London stop in the group’s ongoing world tour, he could be seen gliding around the stage, floating from flawless vocals to faultless choreography, barely breaking a sweat despite the sweltering July heat. Seeing him perform prompts a million questions. How is he doing? Does he enjoy this life? What’s it like being screamed at all the time? Is he happy? Does he have friends outside the band? When does he hang out with them? What do they get up to? What occupies his mind when no one is watching? What does the explore page on his Finsta look like? What was his time in the military like? Did he enjoy it? Is he still in touch with anyone from his unit? What is it like to be recognised by so many but known by so few? The tight-lipped nature of the K-pop industry means that a lot of these questions won’t be answered – at least not here. But what follows is our attempt to get to know this idol, who stands at the very pinnacle of global pop culture. Hi V. How would you describe this current chapter of your life? V: We’ve been really busy [lately] with our BTS WORLD TOUR ARIRANG in Europe, and I’ve had the chance to experience so many different cities along the way. Every place feels unfamiliar at first, but I’ve been finding small moments of happiness that feel comforting and make me feel at home. Your life has been very busy for a long time. What helps you feel grounded? V: What helps me stay grounded when everything moves so quickly is learning to appreciate the present moment. I’m trying to focus on the fact that I can have a good day without always having to rush or achieve something. I’ve realised that, even during a busy life, it’s important to slow down and enjoy where I am right now. I feel most like myself on stage, when I’m able to express who I am through performance V: Right now, while I’m on tour with BTS, what helps me reconnect with myself the most is being on stage. That’s the moment I feel the most like myself, when I can fully express who I am through performance. Another important part is our fans, ARMY. They remind me why I chose this path and help me remember the passion that started my journey in the first place. What do you think you would be doing if you weren’t a musician? V: I’ve thought about it before, but whenever I do it feels a little scary, so I just tell myself to stop overthinking. It reminds me how grateful I am to be making music. I’m happy with the life I have now, so I just try to enjoy each moment and do my best. You were 17 when you debuted with BTS. What advice would you give to your younger self? V: If I could give my younger self one piece of advice, I would tell him to stay focused on music. There may be moments when he becomes curious about things beyond music, and exploring new experiences is important, but I would remind him to always remember why he started this journey and continue to put his heart into music. Has your definition of success changed since you first debuted? V: When I first debuted, I think I had a very simple definition of success. I thought that, if I could appear on TV, that meant I had succeeded. But now I see success a little differently. Being able to share my music and my story with people is still meaningful, but I also think success is about being able to continue doing what I love and being remembered in a positive way. What is the best piece of advice you’ve been given? And who was it that gave it to you? V: One piece of advice that has stayed with me is, ‘You’ve done well, you’re doing well, and things will work out, so get some good rest’. It was something a close older friend told me a long time ago, during a moment when I was lacking confidence and needed some encouragement. I still remember those words, because they gave me comfort when I needed it most. Sometimes, even after all these years, that simple message comes back to me and reminds me to keep going. What was turning 30 like for you? Has your mentality changed since hitting this age? V: Honestly, I don’t think there was a big difference when I entered my 30s. Other than realising I need a little more time to recover than I used to, I don’t feel like much has changed. I’m still the same person, with the same passion and mindset. You’ve often spoken about how important your grandmother was in your life. Is there a particular memory of her that still stays with you today? V: My grandmother is someone who means so much to me. When I was growing up, she always made delicious meals for me, so I don’t really remember having many experiences of eating out until I was in elementary school. I think the first time I had a meal outside was probably my elementary school graduation day. I still remember how special that moment felt, and how much I enjoyed her meals. Looking back, those moments with my grandmother were filled with so much love and care, and they are memories I still cherish today. How would you describe the new BTS album? How would you like it to make people feel? V: ARIRANG is about BTS’s identity and our roots. I believe this album shows our growth and who we have become over the years. During the making of the album, our different personalities and perspectives came together, and I think those differences are what made the music more colourful and honest. Ultimately, we hope ARIRANG becomes a timeless piece of work that can resonate with people across generations and cultures. When I first debuted, I had a very simple definition of success. But now I see [things] differently How would you define your role in the group, musically and also in terms of personality? V: I think of myself as someone who helps to balance the energy within the group. If the mood gets too high, I will try to bring it down and create a sense of calm, and if things feel a little too quiet, I’ll try to lift the vibe. I feel like I help create the right balance. V: I feel the most confident right after a performance. When I walk back into my hotel room after a show, I’m usually filled with so much energy and confidence because I’m still carrying the excitement from the stage. I come back to my hotel, take a shower and get ready to sleep feeling really content and proud, but because the adrenaline is still there it’s not always easy to fall asleep right away. What’s one thing people often assume about you that isn’t quite true? V: I’m a pretty honest person, so I’m not sure if there’s anything people often misunderstand about me. But if there’s something people are curious about or want to know, I’d be happy for them to ask. What are you curious about at the moment? Is there something you’re trying to learn or understand that has nothing to do with your music? V: These days, I’ve been really into learning the piano. It’s something I’ve been enjoying and exploring at my own pace. If we’re talking about something completely unrelated to music, I would say travel. I’m looking forward to a quiet kind of travel where I can slow down, take in new surroundings and have time to enjoy the moment. When people look back on your career many years from now, what do you hope they remember – not just about your work, but about you as a person? V: I hope people remember me as an artist who could express a wide spectrum of emotions. I want my work to reflect different feelings and stories, and I hope those emotions can reach people in their own way. title: Norway bids final farewell to popular King Harald V as crowds and royals converge for his funeral - WECT
content: OSLO, Norway (AP) — Norway bade its final farewell to Harald V on Wednesday as crowds lined the streets and foreign royals and leaders converged on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king, who was remembered as a popular monarch with a down-to-earth touch. A 21-gun salute rang out over the capital at the start of a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral. Harald’s son, new King Haakon VIII, and other senior royals walked behind the coffin, draped with the red Norwegian royal standard. Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, followed in a car. Norwegian officials and foreign dignitaries joined the solemn procession. They included the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Jordan. Also present were the heir to the British throne, Prince William, and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino, as well as political leaders from more than 20 countries, including Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As the funeral service began, Norway came to a halt for a minute of silence. Harald, who died on Aug. 28 aged 89, was Europe’s oldest monarch and had reigned for 35 years. He modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who recently abdicated. His son immediately became king and last week took an oath of allegiance to Norway’s constitution in parliament. The parliament’s speaker, Masud Gharahkhani, said at the service that “King Harald was close to the people” and recalled that “he wasn’t afraid to meet people in his rubber boots.” He remembered Harald saying in his 2008 New Year’s address: “I wish we would stop using the term ‘the weakest in society.’ In reality, some of these people are among the strongest of us all.” “He lived up to his motto: He gave his all for Norway,” Gharahkhani said. Large crowds flocked to Oslo for the funeral, and thousands stood behind barriers on streets lined with national flags. The downtown area was closed to vehicles and electric scooters, and police had instructed people not to bring bicycles, umbrellas or sharp objects. People tuned in across the country of about 5.6 million. Scores of churches, libraries, cultural centers and city halls made big screens available for the public to watch the funeral, public broadcaster NRK reported. The government said it wasn’t an official holiday, but schools and workplaces could individually opt to let students and employees watch. Ahead of the funeral, Norwegians waited patiently to file past Harald’s coffin in the chapel of the royal palace. The queue was seven hours long at one point over the weekend. Over 46,000 people visited the chapel during the week it lay in state. “The love between the people and King Harald has not ended — quite the contrary,” said Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit, who led the funeral service, pointing to the tributes left outside the palace after his death. “The sea of flowers, along with the words and drawings that accompany them, speaks loudly and clearly of a heart so full that it overflows.” After the funeral, Harald’s coffin was taken in a smaller procession to Akershus Fortress, where his predecessors are buried in the crypt of the palace chapel. Haakon followed with the two other Scandinavian monarchs, King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden and King Frederik X of Denmark. Among those who attended the funeral was Mette-Marit’s eldest son and Haakon’s stepson, Marius Borg Høiby, who has no royal title or duties. Høiby is appealing against a rape conviction after a trial earlier this year that cast a shadow over the royal family. Norway’s monarchy traces its origins to King Harald Fairhair in the ninth century. When Norway regained its independence from Sweden in 1905, three-quarters of voters in a national plebiscite approved restoring the monarchy. The Norwegian royal house has kinfolk in other European royal families. Harald and Haakon are related to both Britain’s King Charles III and Spain’s King Felipe VI: They’re all descendants of the U.K.’s Queen Victoria, who reigned from 1837 until her death in 1901. Today, the throne’s role is largely symbolic and power lies with the elected government and parliament, but the Norwegian royal family retains a role in promoting the wealthy Scandinavian nation around the world. content: Manchester United make a welcome return to the UEFA Champions League when facing Sabah on Thursday night. The visitors from Azerbaijan provide the opposition for Michael Carrick’s men, as we look to get off to a good start in the competition, with tickets now available on general sale for all supporters. Add The Busby Babe as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. On the back of conceding an equaliser to Everton with virtually the last kick of the game at the weekend, the Reds are looking to respond positively, with the Manchester derby against City also on the horizon. This is the first time we have faced a team from Azerbaijan and the tie will be our 300th in the European Cup or Champions League, tracing all the way back to 1956. Sabah are coached by Valdas Dambrauskas, who has an interesting story. The Lithuanian appeared on the equivalent of ‘Who Wants to be a Millionaire?’ in his homeland and used his winnings to finance a move to England. Valdas worked for United as an Academy coach, across our UK and international programmes, around 20 years ago. The club’s CEO, Ramin Hasanov, also assisted with our full-time MUSS (Manchester United Soccer Schools) programme in Baku between 2014 and 2018, as part of the club’s partnership with Bakcell. Sabah are in fourth place in the domestic Azerbaijan Premier League table, during the early stages of the campaign, and have a game in hand on leaders Johor. They have enjoyed a remarkable rise over such a short period of time and won their historic first title by finishing nine points clear of Qarabag. United have a 25-man A-List for the Champions League but can introduce players from the B-List, which includes the likes of and Leny Yoro. However, Manuel Ugarte is definitely out due to injury, while Amad, Carlos Baleba and Matthijs de Ligt have also been sidelined. Mason Mount was an unused substitute at Hill Dickinson Stadium and Benjamin Šeško pushed his claims for a starting spot with his goal. Marcus Rashford was withdrawn in the second half, after “feeling a bit of something” according to Carrick. Sabah thumped Zira 5-0 at the weekend, with Rwanda international Joy-Lance Mickels scoring a hat-trick. Serbian striker Veljko Simic looks set to lead the line while Du Queiroz and Tymoteusz Puchacz, among the summer recruits, are in the squad submitted to UEFA. title: The World’s Royals Come Together to Attend the Funeral of King Harald V of Norway - harpersbazaar.com
content: Norway’s oldest reigning monarch passed away in late August at the age of 89 Early this morning, thousands gathered in Norway’s capital city of Oslo for the funeral of King Harald V, who passed away on August 28 at the age of 89. Harald’s reign as the sovereign of Norway began in 1991, following the passing of his father, Olav V. In 2024, he reached the milestone of becoming Norway’s oldest reigning monarch. He is succeeded by his son, Haakon VIII. During his reign, Harald was dedicated to making the royal family more accessible to the Norwegian public, and he also pushed for more modernization within the storied institution. He was even vocal about environmental issues and promoting diversity and inclusion. Today, royals from all over the world came out to pay their respects to the late monarch at his state funeral service, held at the Oslo Cathedral. Prominent figures in attendance included Prince William and aunt Princess Anne. King Felipe, Queen Letizia and Queen Sofía of Spain were also present, as were Prince Albert II and Princess Charlene of Monaco. One royal who notably missed the ceremony was King Charles III, who has lessened his travels since he was diagnosed with cancer in 2024. However, the British sovereign does not traditionally attend the funeral services of other heads of state. (Queen Elizabeth II only attended one during her 70-year reign—for King Baudouin of Belgium in 1993.) Thus, William and Anne represented the family in his place. Other royal figures in attendance included figures from Sweden, the Netherlands, Japan, Belgium, Denmark, Greece, and Jordan. title: Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral - dw.com
content: Heads of state from around the world came to Oslo to pay tribute to the late monarch. A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral. Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king. Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service. The procession and funeral brought an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked  monarch at the age of 89. "He struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth," Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said in his eulogy. "He made Norway greater. He spoke of a 'we' in Norway where everyone is there for each other." After the ceremony, his casket was moved to its final resting place at the royal palace chapel. A private ceremony just for family followed. The funeral was attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. They included the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden. Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are also attending. Indeed, flags were flown at half-mast in Berlin's government in honor of Harald, whose 35-year-reign made him well-known and respected across Europe. Harald's son King Haakon VIII was be there alongside his family including his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit. Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship is also expected to be at the funeral. Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest. title: Forget vinyl v digital debates, this kind of musical ‘authenticity’ brings real rewards - The Guardian
content: Period instruments are miles away from retro affectation, and as two Proms this week will show, can actually bring historical music up to the moment Nostalgia. What a kick. And what a commercial boon for the music industry. Love the sound of 60s pop and 70s disco? You need the original synths if you’re a composer or producer. You listen to music on digital streams? Loser! Join the retro-future of vinyl enthusiasm, and feel the grooves under your fingers like your parents or grandparents used to. Or you can even make music physical again through the horrible medium of cassettes: all that plastic, all those tiny liner notes, all that high-speed dubbing. Retro-futurists cherish what they claim is the extra warmth and sonic richness of vinyl, but there is no acoustic reason why vinyl is better. It is in fact objectively worse as a carrier of sonic information than any high-resolution stream of the same track, song or symphony. For cassette nostalgists, if it’s got that old-fashioned tape hiss, it sounds more “real”. We’re now looking for things to sound less clean. Because we distrust today’s technological utopia, we want signs that our music is less polished, less perfect, and thus more human. But what the recording industry is doing now with its return to vinyl, classical music has been doing for decades. Musicians and musicologists have long been obsessed with learning about the origins of the music they study and play, to experience what the technology of instruments and performing cultures of earlier centuries actually sounded like, whether the 12th-century Germany of Hildegard of Bingen or the 19th-century Vienna of Beethoven and Schubert. David Munrow brought medieval and Renaissance music to the mainstream across TV, radio and recordings in the 1970s and showing what instruments such as shawms and crumhorns could do; Roger Norrington and John Eliot Gardiner set up choirs and ensembles to do the same for 17th and 18th-century music, and Nikolaus Harnoncourt led the charge through the music of later centuries, putting the ethos of early music research into the lifeblood of chamber groups and large-scale symphony orchestras in music from Schubert to Bruckner. But where the claims for vinyl or cassettes’ “authenticity” are bogus when it comes to actual sonic fidelity, it’s different when comparing older instruments in classical cultures and their modern counterparts. Earlier instruments have different qualities of sound and expression. The sound and feel of a harpsichord that Bach was writing for in the 18th century is vastly different to a grand piano made today: the plucked strings of the harpsichord mean that the sound of each note disappears quickly, where a Steinway can create halos and continuities of sound. French horns that can play in any key are taken for granted today, where previous generations had to literally pull their brass instruments apart to play one set of notes or another. It’s a similar story for strings and woodwinds, as earlier generations of musicians had to play with the temperamental realities of gut strings that don’t stay in tune, and reeds that couldn’t be relied on. But the sounds that earlier orchestral instruments make aren’t “worse” in the way that cassettes or vinyl are. Instead, their differences invite other ways of playing for the musicians, and they open up new dimensions of feeling for us. The difference between Bach’s music when it’s played on modern instruments in what is now – ironically – an old-school approach, using vibrato in the strings, lush lyricism in the rest of the orchestra, and full-scale choral forces, compared with the leaner sounds that smaller period instrument ensembles make, isn’t only a difference of soundworld, it’s a gulf of meaning and feeling. Listen to these two performances of the opening chorus of Bach’s Matthew Passion: Karl Richter conducting his massed Munich forces in 1979, and Paul McCreesh leading the Gabrieli Consort in 2003. They’re playing the same piece, but these are radically different experiences. Richter’s reading of the work is about making a vast immovable musical monument, while McCreesh’s – played nearly twice as fast, using just one voice to each part – is an invitation to us as individuals to empathise, to bear witness, to be part of the drama. That’s the key: these are new, contemporary feelings that period instrument performances open up. As the pianist Vikingur Ólafsson said, the idea that if you play on old instruments you’re making the exact sounds that Bach, or Beethoven or Mahler would have heard is neither truly possible, and nor is it the point. Our ears, our bodies, and our whole listening culture is different. (Which reminds me of Janeane Garofalo’s immortal cameo as the “serving wench” Melinda in the medieval-themed restaurant in The Cable Guy: “There were no utensils in medieval times, hence there are no utensils at Medieval Times. Would you like a refill on that Pepsi?”) In the final few Proms concerts of the season you can hear the latest developments of classical’s retro-future explorers, all playing “period instruments”. On Thursday, the musicians of Arcangelo perform Bach’s B Minor Mass on original instruments, and the next night, there’s Mahler’s Ninth symphony from the Mahler Academy Orchestra playing instruments that fit the specifications of the ones that Mahler himself ordered for the Vienna opera in the early 1900s. Period instruments have more grain, more colour, more guttural directness and more lyrical intensity than their modern counterparts and so to my mind are better equipped to reveal the emotional imperfections, ambiguities, and expressive complexities of the music they’re playing. That makes me sound like a cassette-fetishising nerd. Oh dear ... In fact, I’ll go further and say that performances such as the Mass in B Minor and Mahler’s 9th at the Proms will have an authenticity that no recording format, analogue or digital, can reproduce. These are one-off performances that will be made and witnessed by those human beings, true to themselves in every moment. All these historical instruments aren’t really about getting closer to past times but to the power of the present tense. This week Tom has been listening to: On repeat, the Berlin Philharmonic’s Proms with Kirill Petrenko. I know, I’m a broken record on this, but their Elgar and Tchaikovsky was inspired and inspiring: they found new depths of feeling and resonance in every moment. Magic.

title: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Official IKEA Mod Features Matt Berry as a Kallax Storage Companion - IGN
content: What We Do in the Shadows' Matt Berry voices an IKEA Kallax bookcase in a free official Creation for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim. The infamous IKEA storage unit will become a fully-fledged in-game companion, Kallax Storageborn, able to carry your items and prevent you becoming easily over-encumbered. You'll even be able to summon him with a custom Dragon Shout (AYE-KEY-YAH). Yes, IKEA. Why is Berry being roped in to lend his baritone boom to a bookcase? Well, this is an officially-licensed IKEA collaboration that plays on the infamous annoyance of being over-encumbered within the game. But there's seemingly more here than just a simple joke. Not only have Berry's talents been secured, but developer Kinggath Creations has crafted a full quest with two new IKEA-themed dungeons, and a boss fight against the Clutter Golem. Need help assembling your inventory? You'll also be able to wield the Dwemer Allen Key weapon, wear the Meatball Helmet, and gobble meatball food items. "At IKEA, we believe in creating a better everyday life for the many people — and why shouldn't that include their digital lives?" said IKEA exec Kemi Anthony. "Skyrim possesses one of the largest modding communities in gaming, and we saw a space where our expertise in functional storage could make a real difference in this fantasy world. "Matt Berry's distinctive, legendary voice brings theatrics, booming authority and charm to the new Creation. In bringing Kallax to life we hope to not only make a meaningful difference for Skyrim players but doing so with a touch of added IKEA playfulness to delight gamers who've long been bogged down by too much stuff." This isn't Berry's first video game credit, of course. You can hear his dulcet tones right now in LEGO Batman: Legacy of the Dark Knight as Bane, or in the celebrated 2024 British indie adventure Thank Goodness You're Here! It's a busy time for Berry, who is due to appear next year in both Sonic the Hedgehog 4 and A Minecraft Movie Squared. This year, he'll appear as The Fish in a new Bill Hader-starring adaptation of The Cat in the Hat. title: Norway bids final farewell to popular King Harald V as crowds and royals converge for his funeral - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
content: Norway is bidding its final farewell to Harald V as crowds line the streets and foreign royals and leaders converge on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king OSLO, Norway -- Norway bade its final farewell to Harald V on Wednesday as crowds lined the streets and foreign royals and leaders converged on Oslo for the funeral of the long-serving king, who was remembered as a popular monarch with a down-to-earth touch. A 21-gun salute rang out over the Norwegian capital at the start of a funeral procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral. Harald’s son, new King Haakon VIII, and other senior royals walked behind the coffin, draped with the red Norwegian royal standard. Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, followed in a car. Norwegian officials and foreign dignitaries joined the solemn procession. They included the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Jordan. Also present were the heir to the British throne, Prince William, and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino, as well as political leaders from more than 20 countries, including Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. As the funeral service began, Norway came to a halt for a minute of silence. Harald, who died on Aug. 28 aged 89, was Europe’s oldest monarch and had reigned for 35 years. He modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who recently abdicated. His son immediately became king and last week took an oath of allegiance to Norway’s constitution in parliament. The speaker of Norway's parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, said at the service that “King Harald was close to the people” and recalled that “he wasn’t afraid to meet people in his rubber boots.” He remembered Harald saying in his 2008 New Year's address: “I wish we would stop using the term ‘the weakest in society.’ In reality, some of these people are among the strongest of us all.” “He lived up to his motto: He gave his all for Norway,” Gharahkhani said. Large crowds flocked to Oslo for the funeral, and thousands stood behind barriers on streets lined with national flags. The downtown area was closed to vehicles and electric scooters, and police had instructed people not to bring bicycles, umbrellas or sharp objects. People tuned in from across the country. Scores of churches, libraries, cultural centers and city halls made big screens available for the public to watch the funeral, public broadcaster NRK reported. Ahead of the funeral, Norwegians waited patiently to file past Harald's coffin in the chapel of the royal palace. The queue was seven hours long at one point over the weekend. Over 46,000 people visited the chapel during the week it lay in state. The government says it was not an official holiday, but schools and workplaces could individually opt to let students and employees tune in for Wednesday's events. The government advised that “noisy events should be suspended while the funeral is ongoing.” After the funeral, Harald's coffin will be taken in a procession to the palace chapel at Akershus Castle, where the late king's ancestors are buried. After a private ceremony for the Norwegian royals, who will be joined by some of the foreign guests and senior Norwegian officials, the coffin will be lowered into the crypt. title: Forest penalty v Liverpool incorrect, but not for VAR - panel - Yahoo Sports
content: Nottingham Forest should not have been awarded a penalty at Liverpool for Alisson's challenge on Neco Williams, the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has said. But the KMI Panel added that the decision did not reach the threshold for a video assistant referee intervention, so Michael Oliver was correct not to send referee Sam Barrott to the pitchside monitor. Williams was brought down by Alisson after releasing a shot in the 68th minute. Morgan Gibbs-White scored to put Forest 2-1 in front, before Victor Munoz secured a 2-2 draw for Liverpool with an 82nd-minute equaliser. The KMI Panel voted 3:2 that Barrott should not have given the penalty, but supported the VAR outcome 5:0. It is possible for the panel to judge them differently because a VAR intervention has a higher threshold than an on-field decision. title: Marius Borg’s difficult return to the royal fold as familiar faces gather for King Harald V’s funeral - HOLA
content: The Norwegian Royal Court has become the most closely watched of the European monarchies. Much of that is due to the series of events that have shaken the foundations of the Crown involving Marius Borg, who over the last twenty-four months has gained a notoriety that culminated in a court case still underway. What at first seemed like a simple news story ultimately led to a four-year prison sentence that has now, on a preventive basis, confined him to Skaugum Estate. Even so, the death of Harald V has prompted his legal team to request a series of special permissions so that, as Queen Mette-Marit’s son, and the late king’s step-grandson, he can attend the final farewell. That possibility could put him in the same space as the most prominent members of royal families from around the world, who are currently gathered for a private banquet at the Royal Palace in Oslo. The first of those special permissions came when King Harald V’s health suddenly deteriorated and his medical team raised the alarm: “He is in very serious condition,” they stressed in a powerful statement that was swiftly followed by the official communication from the monarch who led the Nordic country for the last thirty-five years. After that downturn, Marius wanted to be present to say a final goodbye to the man who had been his step-grandfather, because Marius has long been treated as another member of the royal family, despite having no title or bloodline. In recent days, the queen’s son has come back into the spotlight, and now his image may reach even further than the House of Glücksburg, into the presence of some of the world’s most prominent royals. On September 9, every representative of the European monarchies is expected at Oslo Cathedral, the very place where, fittingly, the Norwegian queen’s son is also expected to appear. The court case that rocked the Norwegian Royal House concluded in June 2026, when the Oslo court sentenced Marius Borg to four years in prison after finding him guilty of a disturbing criminal record. Although nearly forty charges were initially brought against him, Queen Mette-Marit’s son was ultimately convicted of two counts of rape of individuals in a state of incapacity, abuse and domestic violence against one of his ex-girlfriends, degrading sexual conduct, as well as threats and violating restraining orders. The ruling also included convictions for offenses and possession of illegal substances. All of that, however, was briefly set aside when Harald V’s body was moved from the Red Hall of the Royal Palace to the Chapel — a moment in which Marius joined the members of the Royal Family tasked with carrying the late monarch’s coffin. That move, surprising as it was, revealed just how close Marius Borg remains to the Norwegian royals. Even though he is not King Haakon VIII’s son, he became a resident of the Royal Palace in Oslo when he was still a small child. His presence at the funeral has not been officially confirmed, but NRK, Norway’s public broadcaster, did confirm that Marius Borg has been granted special permission to attend the monarch’s funeral at Oslo Cathedral. If he does go, it will mark the first time he has appeared alongside members of the Swedish Royal Family, who watched him grow up, since being found guilty, as well as with Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary and even Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia. If this potential encounter does take place, it will be a true test for the strict protocol of the Norwegian Royal House. For Sweden’s Crown Princess Victoria or the kings of Denmark, the visual impact of coming face to face, in the middle of a state funeral, with the young man they saw grow up in the palace, and who is now serving a preventive sentence after appealing his devastating conviction, adds unprecedented tension to the occasion. Without a doubt, every gaze will be torn between the solemn tribute to the late king and the presence of Mette-Marit’s son at the most high-profile event of the year. © ¡HOLA! title: Where Will Norway’s King Harald V Be Laid to Rest? - Town & Country Magazine
content: Following his state funeral, the late monarch will find his final repose in Akershus Fortress. On August 28, 2026, King Harald V of Norway, then Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, died at the age of 89. The late monarch’s death came following a period of decline, including multiple hospitalizations and treatment for hemolytic anemia, a blood disease that had caused fluid to accumulate in his body. He was survived by his wife of nearly 60 years, Queen Sonja, as well as their two children, King Haakon and Princess Märtha Louise, and five grandchildren. Memorial services for the late king began on September 1, when Harald's coffin was carried through the Royal Palace in Oslo to the Palace Chapel by members of his family in a solemn procession. The Palace Chapel was then opened for viewing, so members of the public could pay their respects through  September 8. Harald’s official state funeral will take place on Wednesday, September 9 at 1:00 p.m. local time at Oslo Cathedral, after which the late king will make his final journey to the Royal Mausoleum at Akershus Fortress. There, he will be laid to rest among other departed royals. Unlike a typical burial, the Norwegian king will have a particularly grand resting place—a sarcophagus. The design, which was reportedly commissioned in 2024 as a joint vessel for both Harald and Queen Sonja, when her time comes, was created by Norwegian architectural firm Snøhetta, led by architect Kjetil Trædal Thorsen, with a reported cost of 20 million Norwegian kroner (more than $2 million.) It is expected that the sarcophagus—details of which have not yet been released to the public—will be placed in the Akershus burial chapel, alongside the dual sarcophagi of his parents, King Olav V and Crown Princess Märtha, and his grandparents, King Haakon VII and Queen Maud. title: Saxon Woods v Costa [2026] UKSC 21: Good Faith & Directors' Duties Under Section 172 - Crowell & Moring LLP
content:
The UK Supreme Court has unanimously dismissed the appeal of Mr Francesco Costa, former chairman of Spring Media Investments Limited, in the first Supreme Court judgment to consider the scope of the duty under section 172(1) of the Companies Act 2006. The foundational position is that good faith requires honest conduct as well as honest thinking. A director’s genuine belief that they are acting in the company’s best interests will not excuse covert or disloyal conduct in pursuit of that belief. Private equity investors, minority shareholders with exit rights, and multinational groups with UK-incorporated entities each face specific practical consequences that are examined below. In particular, by setting aside the requirement to establish dishonesty under the Ivey test in favour of a broader fiduciary loyalty framework, the Supreme Court has materially widened the range of director conduct that may ground a claim, including in the context of misfeasance proceedings brought by officeholders under the Insolvency Act 1986. Each of these implications is examined below. All company directors, irrespective of the size of the company, have a fiduciary duty under section 172 of the UK Companies Act 2006 to act in good faith to promote the success of the company for the benefit of its members as a whole. Spring Media Investments Limited provided creative services to fashion, beauty, and luxury brand clients. In 2016, its shareholders and the company entered into a shareholders’ agreement requiring all parties to work together in good faith towards a sale of the company by no later than 31 December 2019. The board delegated the conduct of that sale process exclusively to Mr Costa as chairman. Mr Costa instead believed a delayed exit would generate a better return. Rather than raise this with the board, he covertly ensured that no other director had meaningful involvement in the sale process, misled the board into believing the company was fulfilling its obligations under the shareholders’ agreement, and instructed advisers not to pursue a 2019 exit. The delay proved catastrophic: the Covid-19 pandemic destroyed the prospect of a profitable exit from 2020 onwards. Minority shareholder Saxon Woods, holding 22.33% of the shares, brought an unfair prejudice petition seeking a buy-out at the price its shares would have commanded had the agreed 2019 exit been achieved. The trial judge found unfair prejudice but held that Mr Costa had not breached section 172, since he subjectively believed he was acting in the company’s best interests. A conditional buy-out order was made, requiring proof that a sale above US$75 million would have been achieved. The Court of Appeal reversed this and ordered an unconditional buy-out, finding dishonesty on the basis of the Ivey v Genting Casinos test. The Supreme Court unanimously upheld the unconditional buy-out, but on a broader and more significant basis. Good faith is both subjective and objective. The duty to act in good faith under section 172(1) applies to the director’s conduct in pursuit of their belief, not only to the belief itself. A director who is sincere in their view but pursues it through concealment, selective disclosure, or covert management of a delegated process acts in bad faith and is in breach of their fiduciary duty of loyalty. The Ivey dishonesty test has been set aside for fiduciaries. The Court of Appeal found a breach by applying the objective dishonesty test from Ivey. The Supreme Court took a broader approach: where a defendant owes a fiduciary duty of loyalty, the duty itself supplies the relevant analytical framework. Dishonesty may be evidence of a breach, but it is not required. A director cannot escape liability by arguing that their conduct, whilst covert, did not cross the threshold of dishonesty by the standards of ordinary decent people. A significant question remains open. Lord Briggs declined to decide whether a company’s contractual commitment in a shareholders’ agreement conclusively determines what section 172 requires. He indicated that a change of course, even one that involves a breach of contract, may be permissible if decided collectively and openly by the board in changed circumstances. The manner in which any deviation is reached, whether covert or collective and transparent, is the critical variable. This question will be central to the next generation of shareholders’ agreement disputes. The remedy is powerful. Establishing the section 172 breach converted the conditional buy-out ordered at first instance into an unconditional one. The value of Saxon Woods’ shares will be assessed at the pro-rata undiscounted value as at 31 December 2019, reflecting the company before it was affected by the pandemic. This removes the evidential burden on Saxon Woods to prove what would have happened in a counterfactual scenario, i.e., that a $75 million sale would have been achieved. Once a section 172 breach is established, causation arguments that might otherwise limit the remedy fall away, which is an attractive position for a claimant. Boards and directors: Audit all delegated authority for significant transactions to ensure written mandates exist with defined scope, reporting obligations, and escalation triggers. Review board minutes to ensure they record not only decisions but also the reasoning behind them. Any director with a personal financial interest in a transaction being managed at board level should take independent advice on disclosure obligations. Private equity and growth investors: Review shareholders’ agreements and investment documents to assess whether exit obligations are supported by adequate governance provisions. Investor-nominated directors should be briefed on the personal nature of their section 172 duties, which run to the company as a whole, not to the nominating investor. Minority shareholders: Where there are grounds to believe a director is pursuing a strategy that diverges covertly from the agreed board position, the Saxon Woods framework provides a basis for a section 172 claim combined with an unfair prejudice petition, with the potential for an unconditional buy-out at full undiscounted historical value. In-house legal teams in multinational groups: Conduct an audit of UK-incorporated subsidiary governance arrangements to confirm that directors are aware of their personal duties under English law and that significant strategic decisions are properly considered and documented at UK board level. Saxon Woods v Costa confirms that good faith in the boardroom is not simply a question of motive. It requires objectively loyal conduct. The judgment lowers the bar for claimants, removes a key defence for directors, strengthens the position of minority shareholders in exit disputes, and leaves open significant questions about the relationship between shareholders’ agreements and directors’ duties. Reviewing governance structures and documentation now is considerably less costly than addressing these issues once a dispute has arisen. title: Sněť – “V bažinách vědomí” - Everything Is Noise
content:
Release date: September 11, 2026 | Dark Descent Records/Me Saco Un Ojo Records | Bandcamp | Instagram As much as I love tracking down all sorts of weird, off-the-wall death metal, sometimes I just feel like dipping into a band that does the sound the classic way and does it well. Czechia’s Sněť is exactly that type of band. While I was a little slow on the draw in checking them out, their debut album Mokvání v okovech made quite a splash among my circles of metalhead friends. It’s been a long five years since then, so the hype was palpable when Sněť announced their sophomore V bažinách vědomí. And hey, you don’t want to be late to the party a second time, right? Several listens in, and friends, I can assure you all; Sněť‘s return is plain gross in the absolute best of ways. The band is positively awash in that old 90’s death metal power, laying down mordant tremolo riffs, chunky grooves, and the odd dip into queasy doom drudge that has festered into a fine vintage since the genre’s initial surge. The solos are blazing, the vocals could rumble the foundations of the local mausoleum, and the putrid atmosphere is cloyingly dense while still sounding clear enough for every instrument to shine. V bažinách vědomí wastes no time conjuring a vile climate with the grooving stomp of opener “Tíha světů”. A lumbering, heavy intro gives way to a more nimble verse where riffs ooze along just like they did on the classics. “Kladivo ve tmě” takes on a snappier pace building to some eerily echoing, while “Natur” is even more upfront and forceful. To their credit, Sněť also knows when to let off the gas, as the more doomy, dread-leaden “Ve stínu slunce” proves. That’s also a great song in particular to point out that Sněť likewise understands an old adage from the authority on all metal Fenriz; all the best classic death metal knew it had to be just a little bit weird. “Ve stinu slunce” manages that with its strange acoustic guitar and whispered spoken word outro. There’s a decent number of weird quirks cutting the putrid fury of V bažinách vědomí. The crackling fire and forest sounds of “Natur”. The buzzing intro of “Moskyt”, which I assume was named after the world’s most vile and evil bloodsucker. The chanted invocation of “Znetvořená panna” and weird chirps that close it. Sněť may be walking some well trodden trenches across V bažinách vědomí, but they certainly know how to still leave their own twist on things. As for classic death metal tropes; they’re abundant. Sheer fiery aggression dominates many of the album’s tracks, but it always feels fun in that delightful old school way. Do you dig that old style of indiscernible but weirdly cool cover art? V bažinách vědomí has you covered. A gross but still legible logo? Sněť‘s got one of the better ones! A grimy production that feels weirdly comprehensible despite the muddy grave soil that it’s caked in. Yep, you’ll find it here. I feel like it’s not the easiest to elucidate V bažinách vědomí‘s qualities without just running through a list of what makes old school death metal a perennial delight, but then… that’s kind of just Sněť‘s deal. They’re a band of capable, talented musicians who want to write death metal the way that it won all our hearts in the past. They’re not looking to reinvent the wheel, just to give it their own unique tread (and maybe a couple more sharp edges than engineers would advise). The fact that a band like Sněť can still roll into the decrepit old mortuary of old school death metal and still find an idiosyncratic way to dress the place up is honestly impressive. Death metal just ain’t dying, and I reckon it’s thanks to bands like Sněť that we can say that. May the rotting never cease. title: Napoli v Arsenal Preview: Gunners Begin Another Champions League Quest - Yahoo Sports
content: Arsenal begin another Champions League campaign on Wednesday night with a difficult trip to Napoli, looking to take the first step towards going one better after the heartbreak of last season's final. The Gunners suffered a painful penalty shootout defeat in the showpiece last season, but they have responded superbly at the beginning of 2026/27. Mikel Arteta's side beat Manchester City in the Community Shield before taking maximum points from their opening three Premier League matches. Napoli's start has been far less convincing. They opened their Serie A campaign with a 2-0 victory away to Genoa but have since suffered defeats against Como and Inter Milan, leaving them 12th in the table. The match kicks off at 8pm BST on Wednesday, September 9 at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona. UK viewers can watch the game live on TNT Sports 1, with coverage beginning at 7pm, while TalkSPORT 2 will provide radio commentary. Napoli have several injury concerns heading into the game, as per The Standard. Scott McTominay is unavailable after undergoing corrective surgery for a minor heart issue, while defenders Alessandro Buongiorno and Davide Marianucci remain sidelined with knee injuries. Giovane is recovering from groin surgery, with Andre-Frank Zambo Anguissa and David Neres both facing late fitness tests after missing training. Benoit Badiashile could make his full debut following his loan move from Chelsea. One particularly familiar threat for Arsenal could be Kevin De Bruyne. The former Manchester City midfielder has appeared from the bench in Napoli's opening three league games and could make his first start of the season. Rasmus Hojlund, meanwhile, is expected to lead the line and arrives with an impressive Champions League record of eight goals in 13 appearances. Cristhian Mosquera missed Sunday's 2-1 victory over Chelsea with a minor muscle problem and looks unlikely to feature, meaning Ezri Konsa could continue alongside Gabriel in central defence. Jurrien Timber has yet to play this season following minor summer surgery, although he has returned to first-team training and could make the squad. William Saliba remains several weeks away from returning from his back injury. Bruno Guimaraes was an unused substitute against Chelsea following a couple of fitness concerns, but the Brazilian should be in contention to start in Naples. Arsenal's attacking quartet of Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Christos Tzolis and Kai Havertz are expected to start together for the fourth consecutive game. European visitors rarely enjoy an easy night at the Maradona, with Napoli beaten only three times in their last 23 Champions League home fixtures. English clubs have accounted for two of those losses. Arsenal, however, arrive with confidence and momentum after winning all eight league-phase matches last season, including an impressive 3-1 victory against Inter on their previous trip to Italy. The atmosphere in Naples will be hostile, but this Arsenal side have already shown they can handle major European nights away from home. Norway bid farewell to King Harald V on Wednesday, as crowds lined the streets of Oslo and foreign royals and world leaders gathered for the funeral of the long-serving monarch. A 21-gun salute rang out over the Norwegian capital as the funeral procession made its way from the Royal Palace to Oslo Cathedral. Harald’s son, the new King Haakon VIII, and other senior royals walked behind the coffin, which was draped in the red Norwegian royal standard. Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, followed by car. Norwegian officials and foreign dignitaries joined the procession, including the monarchs of Sweden, Denmark, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, Monaco and Jordan. Britain’s Prince William and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino were also present, alongside political leaders from more than 20 countries, including Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. At the end of the religious service, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in a "missing man" formation, as the casket was taken to the Akershus Castle chapel. There it will be lowered into the crypt of the royal mausoleum, next to Harald's parents and grandparents. He will be laid to rest in a $2 million (€1.7 million) sarcophagus whose design remains secret. Once the burial is completed, flags across the country, which were lowered to half-mast after Harald's death, will once again be raised and church bells will ring for an hour. Norway's police force has mobilised nearly 3,000 officers in what it has described as "one of the biggest operations" in its history. Some 3,500 soldiers have also been deployed, while exceptional airspace restrictions have been imposed over much of the eastern part of the country. Until his death, Harald, who ascended the throne in 1991, was the oldest reigning monarch in Europe. Despite mounting health issues in his later years, he had always ruled out abdicating and was extremely popular among Norwegians. Embodying an open and tolerant Norway, he made a deep impression by celebrating diversity in a 2016 speech marking the 25th anniversary of his reign. "Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other," he said, adding: "Norwegians believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing." Thousands of Norwegians filed past the king's casket in the past week, some waiting in line for hours. The square in front of the palace has been covered with flowers, drawings and candles. "He was the grandfather of the nation," said Gunn Johnsen, 81, speaking to the AFP news agency on Tuesday, explaining that she took an hour-long train ride to pay her last respects. "Generous, inclusive, kind," added her friend Vigdis Simonsen, 64. Near the University of Oslo, a large billboard displayed a photo of a smiling Harald with the inscription "Thank you for everything." Almost 72% of Norwegians said they support the monarchy, up by eight percentage points from a previous survey in May, in an opinion poll conducted after the king's death and published last week. Support had dropped to its lowest level in February, when 60% said they were in favour of maintaining the monarchy while 27% were not. At the time, the royal family was embroiled in a series of scandals that damaged its image. Mette-Marit in particular was under heavy criticism for her past ties to the late convicted American sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and her son's legal troubles. While Haakon VIII, 53, is very popular, opinions on the new queen remain deeply divided. title: King Harald V’s final farewell: Inside the historic funeral set to bring Norway to a standstill - HOLA
content: The funeral of King Harald V of Norway will bring together in Oslo Cathedral many of the world’s most prominent leaders. It will involve an extraordinary security operation, the largest in Norway’s history, for what will be the biggest tribute ever paid to a monarch in the country. Tomorrow, on September 9th, Europe’s royal families will come together in the Nordic capital to honor Norway’s recent history, in a ceremony that will also present a new Royal Family to the world: for the first time, they will appear on the balcony of the Royal Palace in Oslo to greet all those gathered in front of the historic building. It will be a moment that intertwines the joy of Haakon VIII’s accession to the throne with the sadness of a final farewell to the man who has reigned over the country for the past thirty‑five years. This Wednesday, September 9th, the world will be plunged into deep sorrow as it bids a definitive farewell to Harald V. On this day, all of Europe’s royal houses will gather in this dynastic setting, where everyone from King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia to King Willem‑Alexander and Queen Máxima of the Netherlands, accompanied by Princess Beatrix and Princess Amalia, will come together for an event that will begin in the early hours of the morning. At that time, a procession led by a military escort will depart from the Royal Palace in Oslo, transporting the mortal remains of Harald V, which have rested there since the day of his death. This procession will be as spectacular as it is symbolic, the crowning touch to a life marked by legend, compassion, and a historic reign. Escorted by the police, the Armed Forces band, the King’s Guard honor company, and the head of the Royal Court, the coffin will leave for Oslo Cathedral. At this point, the King’s family will follow behind the body of Harald V, with members of the royal families attending the Norwegian monarch’s final farewell walking in their footsteps. In an overwhelming silence broken only by the cadence of marching soldiers, the historic procession will advance through the heart of Oslo in an unprecedented display of solemnity. This funeral cortege will become part of the shared memory of Europe’s monarchies, although it will be at 1:00 p.m. when the King’s body is received at Oslo Cathedral and the funeral mass in memory of the sovereign begins. Under the soaring vaults of the magnificent cathedral, the service will be led by Bishop Olav Fykse Tveit, with the distinguished participation of the Bishop of Oslo, following the strict and sober funeral rite of the Church of Norway. Music, the emotional centerpiece of this farewell, will fill the space with the mastery of the cathedral’s cantor and the heavenly voices of the Oslo Cathedral Choir. The service will also include a minute of silence, observed not only inside the cathedral but across the entire country, framed by three solemn tolls of the bells marking the beginning and end of the national mourning. After this powerful moment of reflection, the president of the Storting and the prime minister will deliver heartfelt commemorative speeches in tribute to his legacy, followed by a moving candlelight vigil led by representatives of different faiths and philosophical traditions. Heads of State and queens from across Europe will bear witness to this exceptional event. The guest list for the historic monarch’s funeral has grown in recent days, turning this event into a true summit of Europe’s royalty, one that underscores their deep bonds with one another. Among those attending are King Frederik and Queen Mary, accompanied by Prince Christian and Princess Benedikte of Denmark, who will travel to Norway to join the entire Swedish royal family in a gesture meant to highlight the close ties between the Scandinavian royal houses. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium will also attend, as will King Willem‑Alexander and Queen Máxima, who will be there, together with Princess Amalia and Princess Beatrix, to say goodbye to the late king. In one way or another, these prominent royals share not only institutional responsibilities but also dynastic ties that make them all related to each other; so, in a sense, they will not only be bidding farewell to a sovereign, but also to a relative with whom they share bonds that go far beyond court protocol. However, the list does not end there. Representing Luxembourg, the new Grand Duke and Grand Duchess will travel to Oslo, accompanied by Grand Duke Henri, and will join the heirs to the Japanese throne, Crown Prince Akishino and Crown Princess Kiko, who have also confirmed their attendance at the historic funeral. Prince Albert II of Monaco will be present, as will Prince Alois and Princess Sophie of Liechtenstein, and King Felipe VI, godfather to Princess Ingrid of Norway, and Queen Letizia, who will attend alongside Queen Sofía. As we’ve said, this will be a true summit of reigning houses, one that will shine a light on their shared ties and will also include representation from the British Crown. In keeping with British tradition, King Charles III will be represented by Prince William, who will attend together with Princess Anne. Serbia, one of the non‑reigning royal houses taking part in this historic gathering, will be represented by Crown Prince Alexander and Crown Princess Katherine, as revealed by royal expert Ángel de la Cruz (@implmaterial on X). After the main ceremony, the coffin will be taken in procession to the Akershus Castle Church for a private service with the royal family, Norwegian leaders, and the presidents of Iceland and Finland. There, the coffin will be lowered into the royal crypt to rest alongside the sarcophagi of Haakon VII, Queen Maud, Olav V, and Crown Princess Märtha Louise. Once this ceremony at the fortress concludes, the final phase of the funeral will begin: the King and Queen will step out into the courtyard, flags will be raised once more to full‑staff, a double royal salute will be fired, and church bells across the country will ring for an hour. Afterward, the royal family will return in procession to the Royal Palace. To bring the day to a close, the Crown Princess, Queen Sonja, and Prince Sverre Magnus will appear on the palace balcony, followed by an official reception hosted by the King and Queen for dignitaries, representatives of royal houses, heads of state, and close family guests. A truly majestic occasion that will undoubtedly be one of the most significant royal events of our century. © ¡HOLA! title: Dr. Jason Zhang receives V Foundation grant to uncover how glioblastoma evades treatment - UCLA Health
content:
Jason Zhang, PhD, an assistant professor of bioengineering in the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering and a member of the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center, has received an $800,000 grant from the V Foundation for Cancer Research to investigate how glioblastoma cells become resistant to targeted treatments. Glioblastoma is the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat brain tumor. One of the major challenges is that glioblastoma tumors are made up of many different types of cancer cells. While treatment may eliminate some cells, others can survive, adapt and continue to grow. The award will support Zhang’s research into how glioblastoma cells become resistant to drugs that block important signals that drive tumor growth. Although these drugs can effectively shut down their primary targets, some cancer cells are able to activate alternative pathways that restore the signals they need to survive. To better understand this process, Zhang and his team will use artificial intelligence to design protein-based sensors that act like molecular “flashlights,” allowing them to watch growth signals inside individual living cancer cells during treatment. In collaboration with UCLA scientists Aparna Bhaduri, PhD, assistant professor of medicine and biological chemistry, and David Nathanson, PhD, professor of molecular and medical pharmacology, the researchers will study these cells using patient-derived tumor models designed to capture key features of the brain and the diversity of human glioblastoma tumors. The research could help scientists identify rare populations of glioblastoma cells that are missed when tumors are studied as a whole. Understanding when and where these cells activate backup survival signals may reveal opportunities to combine therapies in ways that prevent cancer cells from escaping treatment. “Understanding how these cells escape treatment is critical for developing better therapies,” said Zhang, who is also a member of the California NanoSystems Institute at UCLA. “This support from the V Foundation will allow us to look at glioblastoma in a fundamentally different way, not as one uniform tumor, but as a collection of individual cancer cells that can respond to treatment in very different ways.” See a doctor, virtually or in-person, with our easy online booking options.
